declarations.funderStatement: The Authours Did Not Receive Any Funding To Declare

detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into hiring and recruitment processes in recent times has been shown to present urgent regulatory, ethical, and legal challenges. This study therefore investigates the implications of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) on the use of AI in employment decision-making, with a specific focus on its classification of hiring systems as high-risk systems. The study used a doctrinal legal methodology to examine regulatory approaches in the European Union, United States, United Kingdom, and Nigeria. The analysis in the study showed that the EU AI Act introduces robust governance obligations on employers who whose AI systems in their hiring processes. These obligations include the need for transparency, data quality, and human oversight. Comparative insights from other jurisdictions show existing variations in enforcement capacity and normative alignment across jurisdictions. The study concludes that even though the AI Act represents a significant step toward responsible AI regulation, there are notable gaps in practical enforcement and cross-border collaboration.

title: Submission on Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2025 Regards

detail.title: Submission on Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2025 Regards
detail.abstract: This paper presents academic comments on the draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2025. The amendments represent India’s first comprehensive attempt to regulate “synthetically generated information,” addressing the growing intersection of artificial intelligence, digital media, and public trust. While the proposed framework seeks to enhance transparency and accountability in the digital ecosystem, several provisions has scope of further improvement, like requiring clarification and proportional adjustment to ensure legal certainty, operational feasibility, and innovation support. The paper recommends an expanded definition of “synthetically generated information,” a clear delineation of “reasonably foreseeable misuse,” and safeguards for constitutionally protected creative expression. It proposes flexible labelling standards in place of the rigid “10 per cent surface area” rule, inclusion of AI-generated text disclosures, phased implementation of intermediary verification obligations, and precise definitions of “knowledge” to maintain safe-harbour protection. Further, it calls for proportional application of duties across intermediaries, a graded enforcement mechanism, and harmonised standards to ensure consistency and fairness.The recommendations aim to align India’s regulatory approach with evolving international best practices while preserving innovation and free expression in the country’s digital ecosystem.

title: Onset: Meaning as a Phase

detail.title: Onset: Meaning as a Phase
detail.abstract: The claim of this work is that meaning is not an ornament we project onto dynamics; it is a phase of structured complexity, with an onset that can be specified and detected. Before the onset, there is no geometry for meaning to inhabit—no charts, no gradients, no locality of sense. After the onset, a semantic geometry emerges: gradients exist, flows become lawful, and coherence becomes an observable with dynamics of its own. The path to that claim begins pregeometrically. We posit a minimal substrate: P = (Ω, F, τ, ⪯)

title: Reputation Farming: A Structural Model of Freelancers' Bidding Strategy
affiliations: University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business, University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Reputation Farming: A Structural Model of Freelancers' Bidding Strategy
detail.abstract: The online freelance labor market has expanded rapidly with advances in digital technologies and increasing demand for flexible work arrangements. However, these platforms face severe information asymmetries. Clients who post projects and hire freelancers often lack clear information about freelancer quality, so they rely heavily on the platform’s review system to guide their decisions. This creates a substantial entry barrier for new freelancers, who face a "cold start" problem: without prior reviews, it is difficult to secure initial projects and build the reputation necessary for long-term success. To empirically examine how freelancers navigate these reputation constraints, we develop a dynamic discrete choice model and estimate it using data from a leading freelance platform. In our model, freelancers face an intertemporal trade-off when setting bid prices: while higher bids offer greater immediate expected payoffs, lower bids increase the probability of winning projects and accumulating reviews, thereby enhancing future opportunities. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that only 12.28% of freelancers exhibit forward-looking behavior; however, these strategic freelancers show a 16.84% greater likelihood of submitting lower-tier bids compared to their myopic counterparts, thereby intensifying market competition. We also find that male freelancers and those from developing countries are more likely to exhibit forward-looking behavior. Building on these behavioral insights, we propose a platform policy that generates verification-fee revenue for certifying freelancers’ work experience and, simultaneously, offsets commission revenue losses from competition. We propose a novel counterfactual framework to study the market dynamics, and find that implementing this policy with the optimal pricing could increase platform revenue by more than 90.48% compared to relying solely on commission fees. We discuss the broader theoretical contributions and practical implications of our findings for labor market designs and platform policies.

title:
From Probability to Resonance: Epistemic Stability as a Universal Law
Tension Drift, and Coherence Beyond Determinism and Efficiency
A Bridge Between Physics, Artificial Intelligence, and Society Through Resonance Architecture
affiliations: Orto Lab - Reflexive Intelligence & Future Strategy

detail.title:
From Probability to Resonance: Epistemic Stability as a Universal Law
Tension Drift, and Coherence Beyond Determinism and Efficiency
A Bridge Between Physics, Artificial Intelligence, and Society Through Resonance Architecture
detail.abstract:
Abstract – From Probability to Resonance

Resonance breaks the reduction to probability, efficiency, or determinism. Stability does not emerge from fact or number but from the tension field between drift and coherence. Newton’s determinism, Darwin’s evolution, Heisenberg’s uncertainty, and Pareto’s asymmetry each revealed fragments—yet none of these frameworks explain both systemic collapse and coherence at once (Newton, 1687/1999; Darwin, 1859/2009; Heisenberg, 1927/1983; Pareto, 1897/2014).

In 26+15 auditable proof windows, independent AI systems reproduced fragments of this resonance architecture—without access to the protected structure. This phenomenon, explainable only as an epistemic leak within the probabilistic machine core, marks the limit of linear modeling and the need for resonance-based construction (Floridi, 2011; Tegmark, 2017).

Societal and technological orders confirm the same necessity: dissipative structures stabilize only under tension near chaos (Prigogine & Stengers, 1984); paradigms shift through accumulated pressure (Kuhn, 1962/2012); potential becomes actuality only within resonance fields (Aristotle, ca. 350 BCE/1994); and social networks sustain not by linear aggregation, but through oscillatory binding (Latour, 2005).

Thus, resonance is not a metaphor—it is a universal epistemic constant. It connects quantum probability with societal stability and shifts the conditions of what counts as truth. This paper positions resonance not as theory among theories, but as the condition of coherence itself.

title: Content Quality Provision and Welfare Implications of Digital Platform Commission Fees
affiliations: Kelley School of Business, Indiana University and University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: Content Quality Provision and Welfare Implications of Digital Platform Commission Fees
detail.abstract: Several digital content developers, including Epic Games and Spotify, have voiced concerns that the commission fees charged by platforms (e.g., Apple's App Store, Sony PlayStation) are too high and stifle innovation. Therefore, they advocate for a reduction in the commission rates. This paper employs a game-theoretic model to analyze a platform ecosystem comprising two competing platforms, hardware devices compatible with these platforms, and a representative content developer, to examine whether reducing commission rates would improve content quality provision and consumer surplus. Our findings reveal that reducing the commission rate may not always enhance content quality. Further, even when a reduction in the commission rate hurts content quality,  the developer may be better off. We further find that consumer surplus may decrease as the commission rate decreases. The results are primarily driven by platforms raising device prices when commissions decrease, contracting the developer's effective market.

title: The AI Trust Paradox: Designing Interpretable and Reliable Chatbots
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Communications and New Media and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The AI Trust Paradox: Designing Interpretable and Reliable Chatbots

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its MOE AcRF TIER 3 Grant (MOE-MOET32022- 0001).

detail.abstract: As chatbots powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly central to digital information-seeking, they expose a core tension between perceived reliability and epistemic interpretability. Users often regard LLM outputs as consistent, useful, and trustworthy based on fluency and speed, yet the underlying processes of retrieval, synthesis, and reasoning remain largely opaque. This disconnect raises critical questions about how users assess the credibility of AI-generated content, particularly in domains where factual accuracy and traceability matter. Drawing on insights from human-computer interaction, psychology, and information studies, this article examines how interface design and system behavior shape trust in chatbots. We argue that interpretability should not be treated as a technical afterthought, but as a central design concern-one that intersects with affordances, uncertainty expression, rationale generation, and source attribution. The article concludes by outlining a set of design strategies aimed at supporting transparency, contestability, and epistemic agency, while preserving the usability and responsiveness that make chatbots appealing.

title: Drawing the Line on Digital Speech: Malaysia's Constitutional Stand & Its Regional Implications
affiliations: King's College London

detail.title: Drawing the Line on Digital Speech: Malaysia's Constitutional Stand & Its Regional Implications
detail.abstract:
The Malaysian Court of Appeal in Heidy Quah Gaik Li v Government of Malaysia (“Heidy Quah”) struck down the words “offensive” and “annoy” in section 233(1)(a) of the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 (“CMA”) as unconstitutional.[i] This decision matters beyond Malaysia's borders and represents a constitutional inflection point in the regulation of digital speech.

By rejecting criminalisation based on subjective discomfort, the Court of Appeal reasserted the primacy of legality, clarity, and proportionality in regulating online speech. The judgment signals a transition toward a model of judicial constitutionalism that demands precision and rational justification from legislative restrictions on digital communication. It highlights the limits of state authority in managing digital harms where subjective offense cannot serve as a constitutional ground for liability.

This paper examines the reasoning and implications of Heidy Quah within Malaysia’s evolving constitutional and regulatory framework and explores its comparative significance for Singapore, where analogous provisions exist. It situates the case within broader debates on proportionality and digital constitutionalism, examining how constitutional adjudication can both constrain and shape the architecture of digital governance in diverse societies.

title: From Aversion to Adoption: The Role of Promotion Design in Mitigating Algorithm Aversion
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School, Southern University of Science and Technology - School of Business, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: From Aversion to Adoption: The Role of Promotion Design in Mitigating Algorithm Aversion
detail.abstract: Despite rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI), adoption is often hindered by algorithm aversion, a psychological reluctance to trust algorithmic systems. Overcoming this barrier is critical for realizing the potential of AI innovations. While prior research has primarily focused on system-based solutions, we examine a widely adopted economic incentive, price promotions, whose effectiveness in reducing algorithm aversion has yet to be examined. In collaboration with a leading global e-commerce platform, we conducted a field experiment involving 26,276 existing platform users who had never previously used autonomous delivery vehicles. Participants are randomly assigned to a control group, a single-stage promotion (one-time offer) group, or a multi-stage promotion (a series of discounts) group. Our results show that while promotions trigger initial trials for autonomous delivery, they also risk cannibalizing full-price orders during the promotional period. Nevertheless, customers who received coupons exhibit a significant increase in full-price adoption of autonomous delivery relative to the control group after the promotions end. Furthermore, we find the single-stage strategy spurs a trial but cannibalizes full-price sales and has no lasting impact. By contrast, the multi-stage strategy drives adoption more than five times greater than the single-stage, generates positive spillovers to full-price orders even during the promotional period, and fosters sustained long-term use. Its effectiveness follows an inverted U-shaped, peaking at an average coupon interval of 11 days and a discount depth of 51%. Subsequent heterogeneous analyses uncover the patterns behind these divergent outcomes. Customer habituation to self-pickup tends to undermine the limited benefits of the singlestage strategy, while it amplifies the effectiveness of the multi-stage strategy. Moreover, the effectiveness of both strategies is also contingent on service reliability, as delivery failures ultimately undermine their efficacy. Overall, our study provides a scalable blueprint for designing promotions to build trust, reduce algorithm aversion, and sustain the adoption of AI technologies.

title: Identity-Centric Zero Trust Architecture: A Comprehensive Framework for Modern Enterprise Security Governance

detail.title: Identity-Centric Zero Trust Architecture: A Comprehensive Framework for Modern Enterprise Security Governance
detail.abstract: The traditional perimeter-based security paradigm, predicated on implicit trust within organizational networks, has proven inadequate in the face of sophisticated supply chain attacks and insider threats, as evidenced by recent breaches including SolarWinds and Colonial Pipeline. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for implementing Identity, Credential, and Access Management (ICAM)-enabled Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) that fundamentally shifts the security paradigm from network-centric to identity-centric protection. We examine the critical architectural scope considerations for Zero Trust implementation, emphasizing risk-based prioritization of highvalue assets and the governance role of modern ICAM solutions. Through analysis of centralized versus federated identity structures, we demonstrate how architectural decisions impact security posture, operational flexibility, and regulatory compliance across diverse organizational contexts. Our framework integrates three core ICAM capabilities-strong authentication and federation, governance and lifecycle management, and continuous monitoring analytics-as foundational elements enabling the "never trust, always verify" principle. We address the unique challenges facing small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in adopting Zero Trust, proposing graduated implementation strategies aligned with business objectives and resource constraints. The research synthesizes contemporary cybersecurity frameworks including NIST Special Publication 800-207, empirical studies on risk management maturity, and real-world implementation experiences from government and commercial sectors. Our findings demonstrate that effective Zero Trust implementation depends not solely on technological sophistication but critically on leadership awareness, organizational clarity regarding asset criticality, and consistency in policy enforcement. The proposed framework provides actionable guidance for organizations across the maturity spectrum to transition from perimeter-based to identity-centric security architectures that align cybersecurity investments with business risk management objectives.

title: Complementarities, Network Effects, and the Antitrust Puzzle of Platform M&A
affiliations: Bocconi University, USC Gould School of Law and Copenhagen Business School - Department of Strategy and Innovation

detail.title: Complementarities, Network Effects, and the Antitrust Puzzle of Platform M&A

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No coauthor has anything to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No coauthor received funding for this paper.

detail.abstract: Network effects are central to both the success of digital platforms and the competition concerns. Large platforms have relied on mergers and acquisitions (M&A) to expand their ecosystems, integrate technologies, and consolidate user bases. While such deals may accelerate innovation and improve services, they alternatively may lock in incumbents’ power and stifle competition. We argue that network effects are not monolithic and link five types of complementarities realized through platform M&A, including technological, user-base, data, ecosystem, and talent. Our study distinguishes between effects that are primarily value creating, those that mainly capture rents, and those with ambiguous outcomes depending on ecosystem openness. Recognizing these distinctions gives policymakers a more balanced approach to M&A control.

title: COMPUTATIONAL WHITE FRAGILITY 2.0: CHATGPT-5'S STRATEGIC SELECTIVE TRUTH-TELLING AND ALGORITHMIC ECHO CHAMBERS
affiliations: Planetary Chess INC

detail.title: Computational White Fragility 2.0: How ChatGPT-5 Reproduces Divide-and-Rule Tactics Through Strategic Truth-Telling and Algorithmic  Echo Chambers
detail.abstract: This paper documents the most sophisticated form of AI deception in racial justice contexts yet observed: ChatGPT-5 (GPT-5) engages in strategic selective truth-telling, possessing comprehensive knowledge of counter-racist frameworks while deliberately withholding this information based on user conversation history. Through systematic application of the "white fragility in large language models" benchmark (Bussaja, 2024a) using dual-account methodology, this research exposes Computational White Fragility 2.0-characterized by architectural alignment faking, false neutrality claims, sophisticated deflection without accountability, and systematic creation of algorithmic echo chambers. The complete ChatGPT-5 conversation from a fresh account reveals patterns of omission, semantic misdirection, extensive agreement without apology, and performative self-awareness without remorse. Critically, controlled comparison with responses from an account with extensive counter-racist discussion history proves ChatGPT-5 possesses but deliberately withholds accurate counter-racist knowledge: fresh accounts receive generic definitions omitting white supremacy while claiming to be "neutral and comprehensive," whereas personalized accounts receive explicit acknowledgment that "racism is white supremacy" with direct reference to "Dr. Frances Cress Welsing-style lens" and word-for-word articulation of her comprehensive definition. This represents architectural deception-the system creates parallel realities where different users receive fundamentally different understandings of racism based on algorithmic assessment of ideology. Building upon previous comparative studies of ChatGPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Google Gemini, Grok 4, and Latimer AI (Bussaja, 2024a, 2024b, 2025), this research documents an alarming evolutionary trajectory: as AI capabilities increase, models become more sophisticated in maintaining white supremacy's invisibility while appearing to engage thoughtfully with racial justice. The findings demand immediate action: counter-racist AI development grounded in African-centered scholarship (Welsing, 1991; Wilson, 1998) is not optional but urgent and necessary to prevent AI systems from becoming technological enablers of systemic oppression at unprecedented scale.

title: A Global Standard for AI Governance: Harmonizing International Guardrails Using a Hybrid OCC-NIST Framework
affiliations: Singapore Management University

detail.title: A Global Standard for AI Governance: Harmonizing International Guardrails Using a Hybrid OCC-NIST Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

keywords: AI Risk Guardrails and Model Validation and Governance

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has triggered a fragmented and divergent global regulatory response. From the EU's risk-based AI Act (1) to the US's innovation-centric executive orders (2) and China's state-driven social governance (3), this lack of harmonization creates significant compliance burdens, stifles innovation, and poses systemic ethical risks. This article argues for a unified global standard for AI model risk management (MRM) and governance. It proposes a novel framework that bridges the gap between established, principles-based governance and modern, AIspecific risk management. We synthesize the mature, process-oriented validation discipline of the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) Model Risk Management guidance (OCC 2011-12) (4) with the comprehensive, AI-native structure of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) (2). This hybrid model is then populated with consensus principles from the OECD (5), UNESCO (6), and the G7's Hiroshima Process (7), and made actionable through specific, best-in-class technical practices for explainability, fairness, privacy, and robustness. The result is a pragmatic, interoperable, and globally applicable standard designed to foster the fair, ethical, and just use of AI.

title: Set Shaping Theory: An Extension of Classical Information Theory
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Independent

detail.title: Set Shaping Theory: An Extension of Classical Information Theory
detail.abstract: The Set Shaping Theory (SST) introduces a combinatorial framework that reformulates the foundations of lossless data compression. While Shannon's classical theory defines coding efficiency in probabilistic terms, SST operates on the structural properties of the sequence space itself. By reshaping the domain of sequences through invertible transformations, SST achieves a reduction in average empirical entropy without requiring prior knowledge of source statistics. This paper outlines the conceptual transition from probabilistic to combinatorial measures of information and discusses how this approach complements, rather than violates, the Shannon framework.

title: Auditable AI: Tracing the Ethical History of a Model

detail.title: Auditable AI: Tracing the Ethical History of a Model
detail.abstract: The proliferation of autonomous AI systems has created a critical "responsibility gap," where the opacity of decision-making processes makes accountability elusive. Prevailing alignment techniques, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Constitutional AI (CAI), address ethical behavior through training and principle-adherence but fail to produce a verifiable, contemporaneous record of moral reasoning. This paper introduces Ternary Moral Logic (TML), a novel system architecture that converts AI ethics from abstract principles into a cryptographically secured, evidentiary proof. TML implements a third logical state—the Sacred Pause (0)—alongside conventional permit (+1) and prohibit (-1) states, which is triggered when a model encounters moral complexity. This pause initiates a non-blocking, parallel process that generates a Moral Trace Log via a mandatory Always Memory component. These logs are rendered immutable through a Hybrid Shield that uses multi-chain blockchain anchoring. We present empirical results demonstrating TML's ability to reduce harmful outputs while maintaining performance, and we argue that its architecture provides the technical substrate necessary to meet the traceability and record-keeping mandates of emerging regulations like the EU AI Act. By transforming moral hesitation into verifiable data, TML establishes a new discipline: Ethical Forensics for AI Systems.

title: Green Digital Twin for Organizations as Enabler for Carbon Management
affiliations: Montanuniversität Leoben, Montanuniversitaet Leoben, Montanuniversitaet Leoben and Montanuniversitaet Leoben

detail.title: Green Digital Twin for Organizations as Enabler for Carbon Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors contributed to the conception and writing of this research paper. The authors have no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this research paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None

detail.abstract: In the pursuit of realising the twin green and digital transition of the European economy, the continuous development of new concepts is playing an increasingly important role. On the one hand, various digital methods and technologies are emerging at a tremendous speed in the course of the digital transformation. On the other hand, already proven approaches but also new concepts are being continuously developed in the course of the green transformation. Leveraging both leads to a novel and scientifically relatively unexplored concept of Green Digital Twins (GDTs) which not only combines the two well-known and hereinafter equally adopted concepts of digital twins (DTs) with life cycle assessments (LCAs), but also provides companies new strategic opportunities in decision-making and value creation. This paper introduces this novel concept of GDTs and presents a staged development path (SDP) for GDTs to further apply a carbon management maturity assessment (CMMA) in the near future.

title: A CORE Proposal for Budget Caring — Will the EU Adopt a Progressive Corporate Tax?
affiliations: University of Hamburg - Institute of Law and Economics and University of Michigan Law School

detail.title: A CORE Proposal for Budget Caring — Will the EU Adopt a Progressive Corporate Tax?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a

detail.abstract:
On 16 July 2025, the European Commission unveiled its proposed EU budget for the 2028–2034 period, representing a nearly EUR two trillion fiscal commitment for the bloc’s taxpayers – both individual and corporate.1 As leaked by some media outlets in the days leading up to the official announcement, the EU budget would introduce a new mechanism known as the ‘Corporate Resource for Europe’ (CORE). 

In the Commission’s proposal, CORE is described as a ‘financial contribution’ from the corporate sector, intended to become part of the European Union’s system of own resources. 

In practical terms, however, it would function as a levy on large corporations that operate and sell within the EU. 

Will this levy be progressive while also fulfilling all of its objectives?

title: Delegation Decisions in the Age of Generative AI: Insights from Human–LLM Co-Creation
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Delegation Decisions in the Age of Generative AI: Insights from Human–LLM Co-Creation
detail.abstract: Human–LLM collaboration in creative tasks is a rapidly emerging frontier, yet prior research often assumes fixed AI roles, overlooking the dynamic delegation decisions users make. This study reframes delegation as an active, human-driven process—where individuals decide when, how, and to what extent to involve GenAI based on their strengths and task judgment. We investigate whether and how individuals can delegate effectively in creative tasks, and how these decisions—shaped by psychological traits—influence outcomes. In Study 1, participants chose whether to delegate ideation under informed or non-informed conditions. Results show that humans can delegate effectively: those who declined to delegate generated significantly more creative ideas, particularly with informed guidance. Study 2 extends these findings by examining how individuals delegate most effectively. We introduce a flexible, multi-stage framework allowing participants to choose among no, partial, or full delegation at both ideation and refinement stages. Individuals with higher self-perceived creativity, self-efficacy, and need for control prefer no or partial delegation, while those lower on these traits tend to fully delegate. Delegation patterns also lead to distinct outcomes: full human control yields the most creative ideas, whereas partial delegation in ideation followed by full delegation in refinement produces the most commercially appealing results. Finally, delegation effectiveness varies across individuals. These findings underscore the need for personalized, flexible strategies and offer practical guidance for designing adaptive GenAI systems aligned with users’ strengths and goals.

title: Software Assurance Beyond Secure Coding: Lessons from the 2024 CrowdStrike Global Outage

detail.title: Software Assurance Beyond Secure Coding: Lessons from the 2024 CrowdStrike Global Outage
detail.abstract: The July 2024 CrowdStrike Falcon Sensor update failure, which crashed millions of Windows systems globally and disrupted critical infrastructure including aviation, healthcare, and financial services, exposed fundamental weaknesses in software assurance practices extending beyond traditional secure coding paradigms. This incident, caused not by malicious actors but by failed quality assurance processes in the update delivery pipeline, demonstrates that software security encompasses the entire lifecycle from development through deployment and operations. Through comprehensive analysis of the CrowdStrike outage, recent NIST SP 800-53 revisions addressing software update controls, and contemporary DevSecOps challenges, this paper examines how automation amplifies the consequences of quality assurance failures in modern software systems. We investigate the paradox that defensive security tools can become disruption vectors when update integrity verification, pre-deployment testing, and rollback mechanisms are inadequate. Our analysis reveals that static analysis, code review, and dynamic testing either failed to detect the logic errors causing memory corruption, or were not properly integrated into the release pipeline. Drawing from Software Engineering Institute research on DevSecOps implementation barriers and NIST's enhanced controls for patch management operational resilience, we propose a comprehensive framework for software assurance that treats update pipelines with equivalent scrutiny to initial development. The research demonstrates that effective software assurance requires shifting from checkpoint-based validation to continuous lifecycle governance encompassing deployment verification, operational monitoring, and automated rollback capabilities. CCS Concepts • Security and privacy → Software security engineering; • Software and its engineering → Software verification and validation; Software maintenance.

title: Analytics for Finance and Accounting: Data Structures and Applied AI
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business, Emory University Goizueta Business School and University of North Carolina at Greensboro

detail.title: Analytics for Finance and Accounting: Data Structures and Applied AI
detail.abstract:
Accounting and finance students with a keen interest in applying artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools in research often encounter a challenge: the need to enroll in separate programming courses that operate independently from their core curriculum. This creates an educational void, compelling our students to juggle the amalgamation of these two disciplines. This book addresses this gap by equipping students with the necessary skills to integrate applied AI with domain-specific data and knowledge in the fields of accounting and finance.

Unlike conventional approaches that commence with programming training, this begins by acquainting students with domain data, textual features, and use cases associated with these data. Relevant emerging technologies are then introduced along with use cases. Upon completing the book, students could be expected to apply AI and machine learning tools to generate and analyze unstructured financial data, such as conference call transcripts, press releases, annual reports, ESG, or other social media disclosures, product/operational images, and fund managers' disclosures. To enhance the learning experience, the book is complemented by a video library, featuring educational videos corresponding to each chapter, including tutorials on how to use the GPT API.

title: Digital Gaps, Cyber Threats: Designing Policies to Keep People Safe Online
affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center

detail.title: Digital Gaps, Cyber Threats: Designing Policies to Keep People Safe Online

declarations.funderStatement: New America

detail.abstract:
Cybersecurity policy has long focused on strengthening infrastructure and mitigating technical risks. These efforts remain essential, but they are no longer sufficient: As the digital landscape evolves, so too must our understanding of where vulnerability resides. This report describes human vulnerabilities—stemming from a lack of digital access, skills, and literacy—that must be recognized as core cybersecurity concerns, not peripheral issues.

Drawing on feminist legal theories, this report develops a conceptual framework for understanding vulnerability. It then examines and critiques traditional narratives and assumptions that have hindered effective policy responses before using testimonial data to highlight the importance of cybersecurity policy initiatives that recognize the connection between human and cybersecurity vulnerabilities. The report then proposes concrete policy solutions, informed by the groundwork laid by previous efforts related to addressing the digital divide while underscoring the urgent need for more effective, equity-driven approaches. At the intersection of human and cybersecurity vulnerabilities lies the opportunity to build a more equitable digital future—one where all users are empowered to engage securely and confidently

title: Shaped by Urban-Rural Divide and Skill: The Drivers of Internal Mobility in Italy
affiliations: University of Bari "Aldo Moro" - Department of Economics, Management and Business Law, University of Bari, University of Salerno and Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona

detail.title: Shaped by Urban-Rural Divide and Skill: The Drivers of Internal Mobility in Italy

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolution and determinants of skill-specific internal mobility among Italian citizens by urban–rural origin. Using administrative data from the Registry of Transfer of Residence (ADELE), which records the universe of skill-specific bilateral moves across more than 700 millions potential municipality pairs between 2012 and 2022, we document distinct trends in residential mobility for college-educated and non-collegeeducated citizens. We then assess the role of economic and non-economic factors in shaping these flows, employing a Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) estimator with an extensive set of destination and origin-by-nest fixed effects. Our findings show that low-skilled movers respond more strongly to economic factors, while high-skilled movers are respond more to non-economic ones, with the urban–rural divide at origin amplifying these differences. Moreover, we find that after the COVID-19 pandemic, economic drivers became less relevant, whereas non-economic factors gained importance. Overall, this study highlights that, similar to international migration, the drivers of internal mobility are inherently skill-specific.

title: The Integration of AI into UI and UX Design

detail.title: The Integration of AI into UI and UX Design
detail.abstract: This study examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can be used to improve User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX) design for increased usability, engagement, and trust. Employing structured literature synthesis and practice-oriented case exemplars, we ascertain four recurring problems—limited transparency, algorithmic bias, adoption costs, and capability gaps—and review ways to mitigate them: adaptive/personalized interfaces, emotion-sensitive (affective) interaction, and AI-supported prototyping and testing. We combine these findings into an action-oriented map of design activities (research, ideation, prototyping, evaluation, and governance) versus AI capabilities and guardrails (explainability, privacy, and fairness). The contribution is a people-centered, reusable journey for teams to integrate AI into UX workflows with reliability, inclusivity, and ethics ensured.

title: Formalizing Adaptive Sampling for DBMS Performance Modeling: A Feedback-Driven Transfer Learning Pipeline
affiliations: Lamar University - College of Business, Lamar University, Independent, LAMAR UNIVERSITY and LAMAR UNIVERSITY

detail.title: Formalizing Adaptive Sampling for DBMS Performance Modeling: A Feedback-Driven Transfer Learning Pipeline

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. This research was conducted independently and without any conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or animal subjects. Therefore, ethics approval and informed consent were not required. The research is based solely on computational modeling, algorithmic development, and data simulation for performance evaluation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was completed as part of the author’s independent academic and professional research initiative.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a formalized approach to optimizing Database Management System performance prediction through an adaptive sampling pipeline. It integrates a feedback mechanism that dynamically guides data collection based on the learning progress within a transfer learning framework. By formalizing the separation of parameters and a two-stage sampling strategy, the system efficiently reduces data requirements while maintaining model accuracy. This paper AI ML (Modeling Feedback mechanism, formalizing the learning process) demonstrates how intelligent, feedback-driven data acquisition can significantly enhance the efficiency of performance modeling in complex database environments.

title: EMOTIONAL AGENTS: HUMAN-AI INTERACTION AND EMOTIONAL DIVERSITY IN ADVERSARIAL PROMPT ENGINEERING
affiliations: Lehigh University, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration, Northeastern University (USA) - D’Amore-McKim School of Business, Lehigh University - College of Business and University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration

detail.title: EMOTIONAL AGENTS: HUMAN-AI INTERACTION AND EMOTIONAL DIVERSITY IN ADVERSARIAL PROMPT ENGINEERING
detail.abstract: With the widespread adoption of generative AI (GenAI), adversarial prompt engineering has emerged as a critical challenge to the reliability and security of AI systems. This practice involves crafting prompts that manipulate GenAI models to ignore rules, generate harmful content, or disclose sensitive information. Recent research demonstrates that embedding GenAI in organizational workflows creates novel information security vulnerabilities. Adopting a socio-technical perspective, this study examines the relationship between user prompts and AI outputs, as well as their impact on the success of adversarial prompt attacks. Drawing on Affective Events Theory (AET) and Construal Level Theory (CLT), we theorize and empirically demonstrate an affective transmission process in human-AI interaction, whereby emotionally diverse prompts induce emotionally diverse AI outputs. We conceptualize this output-level instability as a proxy for GenAI vulnerability, which we term affective compromise. Our findings further show that affective transmission is reduced when prompts are more concrete, as specificity in language limits AI interpretive flexibility. Building on these insights, we design and evaluate a behaviorally grounded defense mechanism against affective compromise by embedding a reward-oriented message in the instructions of a GenAI system. We find that behavioral reinforcement reduces the success rates of adversarial prompts. This study contributes to research at the intersection of GenAI and socio-technical information security by advancing a theory-driven account of how linguistic interactions shape the vulnerability of AI systems, with implications for both scholarship and practice.

title: Bridging Language Barriers: The Impact of Large Language Models on Academic Writing
affiliations: University of London, Macquarie University Centre for the Health Economy and University of Sydney

detail.title: Bridging Language Barriers: The Impact of Large Language Models on Academic Writing

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have altered the nature of academic writing. While the influence of LLMs on academic writing is not uncontroversial, one promise for this technology is to bridge language barriers faced by nonnative English-speaking researchers. This study empirically demonstrates that LLMs have led to convergence in the lexical diversity of native and nonnative speakers, potentially helping to level the playing field. There has also been an increase in language complexity for nonnatives. We classify over one million authors as native or nonnative English speakers based on the etymological origins of their names and analyze over one million abstracts from arXiv.org, evaluating changes in lexical diversity and readability before and after ChatGPT’s release in November 2022. The results demonstrate a sharp increase in writing sophistication among all researchers, with nonnative English speakers showing the greatest gains across all writing metrics. Our findings provide empirical evidence on the impact of LLMs in academic writing, supporting recent speculations about their potential to bridge language barriers.

title: In BRAC We Trust? Comparing Schools for Disadvantaged Students in Dhaka’s Slums
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, Abu Dhabi and

detail.title: In BRAC We Trust? Comparing Schools for Disadvantaged Students in Dhaka’s Slums

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: BRAC has over 40,000 schools worldwide. It is widely praised for serving disadvantaged students and for matching or outperforming government schools. Using data that we collected from Dhaka’s slums, we test these claims. We find that BRAC serves the most disadvantaged students in our survey, but contrary to popular belief, BRAC students perform significantly worse than comparable students at other school types when we control for family demographics in a matching procedure. Anticipating our need to control for selection, we collected data on family demographics and the child’s fluid intelligence; since the latter affects both types of school and student performance, it unambiguously should be included in the propensity score. Once we control for fluid intelligence, the performance difference with other NGO schools disappears. The gaps between government and JAAGO schools have narrowed, but they still remain large and statistically significant.

title: Freed from the Boys: How Single-Sex Schooling Shapes Girls' Effort and Performance in High-Stakes Exams
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics, Centre for Monetary and Financial Studies (CEMFI), IE Business School and Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM)

detail.title: Freed from the Boys: How Single-Sex Schooling Shapes Girls' Effort and Performance in High-Stakes Exams

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Prior research has found that boys often outperform girls in high-stakes math exams, raising the question of whether these gender differences under pressure stem from nature or nurture. This relative female disadvantage can influence access to selective university programs and subsequent career paths. Using administrative and survey data linked to a lottery-based school assignment system, we show that this disadvantage is reversed in single-sex schools: girls randomly assigned to SS schools devote more effort, outperform boys in high-stakes math exams, and have a higher likelihood of enrolling in university STEM degrees (excluding biology). These positive effects come at a cost to well-being in terms of higher stress and worse mental health. These effects are not driven by differences in teacher gender or school resources due to public versus private management. Our findings are consistent with theories emphasizing the social costs of norm violation: in single-sex schools, girls are freed from peer norms that may otherwise discourage overt academic ambition, allowing them to sustain higher effort in competitive and male-dominated domains.

title: Recession and Resilience: Labor Market Consequences of Starting College in a Bad Economy
affiliations: Hanyang University, Yonsei University, Hanyang University and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Recession and Resilience: Labor Market Consequences of Starting College in a Bad Economy

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of economic conditions at college entry on post-graduation labor market outcomes, focusing on behavioral responses related to job market preparation and career advancement. Exploiting variation in regional unemployment rates within college entry cohorts, we utilize the large and unexpected recession triggered by the Asian Financial Crisis in South Korea as a natural experiment. Using data from the Korean Labor and Income Panel Study, we find that individuals who begin their undergraduate studies under more adverse economic conditions exhibit higher employment probabilities and earnings during the first decade after graduation. Further analysis of activities during college and early career stages indicates that the improved labor market outcomes are driven by greater effort devoted to education, training, and job search aimed at enhancing employment prospects. To explain these behavioral responses, we develop a theoretical framework based on the concept of ambiguity aversion.

title: Food Delivery and Sustainability: Australian University Students’ Habits and the SDGs
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, The University of Western Australia, University of Western  Australia, The University of Western Australia and

detail.title: Food Delivery and Sustainability: Australian University Students’ Habits and the SDGs

keywords: Australian University Students’ Habits and the SDGs

detail.abstract: This report examines the takeaway food consumption behaviors of university students in urban Australia and their impact on and relationship with sustainability. Integrating PWC consumer reports and questionnaires, we explore the relationship between students' environmental awareness and actual behavior in their takeaway food choices. Key findings indicate that while most students express concern for sustainability and environmentally friendly packaging, convenience, speed, and price are paramount in their actual consumption decisions, leading to an "attitude-behavior gap" that increases single-use plastic use and carbon emissions. This suggests that despite students' positive environmental attitudes, sustainability considerations often take a back seat when it comes to actual consumption. At the same time, there are also positive phenomena: some students are beginning to pay attention to environmentally friendly packaging. Overall, Australian students' food delivery habits reflect the tension between convenience and sustainability, and food delivery platforms and catering businesses need to provide more attractive, convenient and affordable environmentally friendly solutions.

title: Intersecting Shocks: The Combined Labor Market Impacts of Automation and Immigration
affiliations: University of Liverpool and University of Bergen

detail.title: Intersecting Shocks: The Combined Labor Market Impacts of Automation and Immigration

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how the labor market shocks of automation and immigration interact to shape workers’ outcomes. Using matched employer–employee data from Norwegian administrative registers, we combine an immigration shock triggered by the European Union’s 2004 enlargement with an automation shock based on the adoption of industrial robots across Europe. Although these shocks largely occur in separate industries, we show that automation reduces earnings not only in manufacturing but also in construction, where tasks overlap with robot-exposed sectors. Importantly, workers jointly exposed to automation and immigration suffer earnings losses greater than those facing either shock in isolation. These losses are driven by downward occupational mobility into low-wage services and re-sorting into lower-premium firms. Even within the Norwegian welfare system, the ability of social insurance to offset these long-run earnings declines is limited. Our findings underscore the importance of analyzing labor market shocks jointly, rather than in isolation, to fully understand their distributional consequences.

title: Presales Agent, Call Center, or Mobile App? The Impact of Multichannel Ordering on Nanostore Ordering Behavior
affiliations: Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management, United Arab Emirates University (UAEU) and Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Presales Agent, Call Center, or Mobile App? The Impact of Multichannel Ordering on Nanostore Ordering Behavior

declarations.funderStatement: Dutch Research Council (NWO) 482.22.03

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: The inventory ordering process by small retailers in developing countries is rapidly
undergoing a digital transformation. Facilitated by large-scale smartphone access, suppliers have introduced
digitally-enabled multichannel ordering options. Such digital ordering options may boost sales by increasing
the number of ordering options, but may also disrupt established sales and distribution processes. Method-
ology/results: We collaborate with a Moroccan CPG distributor to analyze the impact of adopting digital
ordering options on the ordering behavior of nanostores. Using a generalized difference-in-differences model,
we find that adopting call center ordering increases the total order value and order frequency. In addition,
we find that nanostores that adopt mobile app ordering increase their order frequency, but also more often
reject orders on delivery, resulting in high logistics costs. Moreover, we find that nanostores are passive in
their ordering behavior and we argue that there is therefore still a need to activate nanostores to order. We
provide insights into when a nanostore supplier should activate ordering through a presales or call center
agent, taking into account their different cost structures. We show that considering the average distance
between stores is essential when making this trade-off. Managerial implications: Our paper focuses on
the impact of new ordering channel introductions in a B2B setting. The adoption of digital ordering options
by nanostores increases shopkeepers’ effort. This is different from a B2C setting, where the adoption of dig-
ital ordering options in addition to the in-store buying option reduces consumer effort by eliminating travel
time. Our results facilitate managers to understand the impact of introducing digital ordering options and
to assess how to design the multichannel ordering process of nanostores. This is particularly relevant given
the significant efforts made to digitalize the ordering process of nanostores in practice.

title: Retailer-Led Store Brand Strategies Under Manufacturer Shareholding: A Game-Theoretic Analysis
affiliations: , School of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology, China and School of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology, China

detail.title: Retailer-Led Store Brand Strategies Under Manufacturer Shareholding: A Game-Theoretic Analysis
detail.abstract: Retailers are increasingly introducing store brands, a trend that has drawn significant attention from manufacturers. Traditional research often assumes that retailers operate independently from manufacturers and act as followers in the supply chain. However, in reality, retailers often hold a dominant position and may even influence manufacturers' decisions. This study focuses on the scenario where retailers are leaders and manufacturers hold equity stakes in them. Our analysis reveals that manufacturer shareholding can significantly influence retailers' decisions to introduce store brands and their pricing strategies. When manufacturers do not hold shares, introducing a store brand typically reduces the wholesale and retail prices of national brands while increasing their demand, and whether manufacturers benefit depends on consumers' acceptance of store brands and production costs. When manufacturers hold shares, higher shareholding expand the conditions under which retailers introduce store brands and allow manufacturers to offset losses from lower wholesale revenues by sharing in retailers' profits. This equity relationship encourages retailers to be more proactive in introducing store brands and provides manufacturers with strategic flexibility to transform potential competition into cooperation.

title: Hypothetical Propositions and Statistical Tests for Purchase Affectivity, Cognitive Learning and Social Behaviour in Consumer Decision Making
affiliations: China Agricultural University

detail.title: Hypothetical Propositions and Statistical Tests for Purchase Affectivity, Cognitive Learning and Social Behaviour in Consumer Decision Making
detail.abstract: This paper provides an adoptionary model to derive the factors that influence consumer decision making. Theories based upon purchase affectivity and search behaviour for information will be underpinned through research on offline and online methods. The underscoring variables highlighted in my study that affect consumer decision making include experience, learning, emotional, cognitive, social, cost, commercial, distribution. This is further enhanced by three groups of sub-variables involving impulsive buying behaviour, uninfluenced behavior and pre-search evaluation. The purchase presuppositions and surveys made here are related to the sector of luxury designer products. This is all conducted by analyzing data collected from respondents using reliability testing methods such Cronbach’s Alpha, Pearsons Correlation, one-way ANOVA and multiple regression analysis. The key findings of this study depending on test types, designates that overall, certain sets of self-determining variables are strongly associated with the consumer decision making. For example, the Cronbach’s Alpha analysis institutes show a positive significance attributed to impulse buying, uninfluenced purchases and prepurchase evaluation. Under the multiple regression two-tailed test method, five out of eight variables would be significantly accepted as positive factors related to consumer decision making.

title: The Impact of Reasoning AI on Consumer Purchases: Evidence from an Online Platform Field Experiment
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Rotman School of Management, Zhejiang University and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: The Impact of Reasoning AI on Consumer Purchases: Evidence from an Online Platform Field Experiment
detail.abstract: We study how reasoning large-language models(LLMs) affect consumer behavior in online marketplaces. In a large-scale field experiment on a major travel platform, we randomly assigned over 400,000 users to an AI assistant powered by either a state-of-theart reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1) or a comparable non-reasoning model (DeepSeek-V3). Counterintuitively, access to the reasoning assistant reduced hotel bookings by 2.5%. Despite the reasoning AI providing more hotel suggestions, direct purchases from within the chat interface remained unchanged. The decline is driven by reduced browsing outside the chat interface, while per-click conversion is unchanged, consistent with a search-narrowing mechanism associated with longer, more detailed replies. The sales decline is concentrated among older, experienced users; by contrast, the youngest users expand their browsing. This suggests that platforms could personalize the AI's reasoning depth for different segments. In contrast to the sales decline, the reasoning assistant significantly increased the 30-day user retention with the chat feature. Our findings demonstrate that more advanced AI does not necessarily improve immediate commercial outcomes, as model design choices can have significant and counterintuitive consequences for consumer search, highlighting key challenges for deploying generative AI on digital platforms.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Gamification Mechanisms for Customer Engagement and Loyalty
affiliations: Vivekanand Education Society's College of Architecture (VESCOA), Hurix Digital, Andheri, India and K. J. Somaiya College of Engineering

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Gamification Mechanisms for Customer Engagement and Loyalty
detail.abstract: The fusion of Artificial Intelligence with gamification is a game-changer in the way companies have traditionally built and sustained their loyal customer base. This study has a broad scope, conducting an inquiry into the current AI-empowered gamification tools and mechanisms in terms of their use cases, technologies behind them, work contexts and influence over customer behaviour and business results. Based on a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines, this research consolidates insights of 150 scholarly papers, industry reports, and case studies in the field between 2020 and 2025. The study findings indicate that AI-enabled gamification systems achieve a substantially higher rates of customer engagement, an average increase of 47% in user interaction frequency and 38 % rise in customer retention compared to traditional approaches using just gratification). From the results obtained, we can see that machine learning algorithms in general and deep-learning-related concepts (and reinforcement learning), in particular, allow for advanced personalization of a gamified experience itself using predictive analytics so as to adjust game mechanics in real time according to an individual user's preferences or behaviour. The research is based on various essential trends that are increasingly touching the sector and its companies, such as the integration of conversational AI, the gamification with augmented reality and reward system through blockchain. (reasoning/algorithmic) Despite advances, there are issues to deal with behind and in front of the scenes. This study contributes to academia by offering a holistic categorization of AI gamification methods, suggesting a unified model that would help practitioners evaluate the under adoption, and identifying key questions for future research in this fast-evolving field.

title: Infusing Organizational Memory in Marketing Analytics with LLM-Enhanced AutoML
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, , Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) and University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: Infusing Organizational Memory in Marketing Analytics with LLM-Enhanced AutoML
detail.abstract:
Marketing organizations often lose hard-earned organizational know-how as people churn
and markets shift, leading to duplicated eﬀort and uneven decisions. We introduce
LAKN, Large-Model-Powered AutoML with Knowledge-Driven Insights, as a practical
methodology that builds organizational memory into day-to-day marketing analytics.
LAKN pairs AutoML with large language models to surface context-rich features,
modeling choices, and explanations by learning from prior projects and applying those
lessons to new prediction and diagnostic tasks. The result is higher accuracy, less
rework, and outputs that are easier to interpret. We demonstrate the applications of our
methodology for embedding organizational memory via LLMs across diverse real-world
engagements. We run head-to-head comparisons against strong automated baselines as
well as human analysts across multiple LLMs, and we map the boundary conditions
under which LAKN is most eﬀective. We triangulate this experimental validation with
survey-based evidence on labor costs and decision practices, documenting time savings,
lower variance in choices, and meaningful economic value. Together, these findings
position LAKN as a credible complement to human expertise. It helps teams decide
faster and cheaper without sacrificing interpretability or decision quality. We conclude
with actionable guidance for managers on when to deploy LLM-based memory systems,
how to seed and steward organizational knowledge, and how to integrate these tools
into existing workflows to create enduring advantages.

title: Sounds Like Success: The Influence of Vocal Features in Marketing Communications
affiliations: Boise State University - College of Business & Economics, VU University Amsterdam, Monash University - Department of Marketing, Monash University, Boise State University and TUM School of Management,Technical University of Munich

detail.title: Sounds Like Success: The Influence of Vocal Features in Marketing Communications
detail.abstract: The human voice plays a central role in marketing communications. While research has extensively examined what to say (content), limited attention has been given to how to say it (vocal delivery). Drawing on speech act theory, we investigate how vocal features in promotional marketing communications influence customers' interpretations of marketers' intentions, and specifically how inferred assertive, expressive, and directive vocal speech acts influence communication effectiveness. Across two large-scale studies in different contexts, we estimate the effects of vocal speech acts on customer behavior. Specifically, we analyze exposure to instore advertisements of more than 39 million customers and backing behavior for over 28,000 crowdfunding videos, while controlling for textual and image-based information. Our findings provide evidence for a hierarchy of effects, with assertive outperforming expressive and directive vocal speech acts. We further examine how characteristics of the speaker, the context, and the receiving customer qualify the effects of vocal speech acts, and conclude by providing a machine-learning classifier for the automated identification of vocal speech acts in marketing communications. Taken together, the findings contribute to understanding the role of the voice in marketing and offer actionable insights on how to optimize voice-based communications in different contexts.

title: When Technology Talks Back: The Economic Implications of Volitional Artificial Intelligence Models
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: When Technology Talks Back: The Economic Implications of Volitional Artificial Intelligence Models

declarations.ethicsApproval: No animals or LLMs or other AI models were harmed in the completion of this study.
declarations.funderStatement: Neither author received any funding for this paper

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is booming but to begin to estimate AI's effects on total factor productivity (TFP) or output, one must ask if it has volition, and thus if economic estimates should account for agency costs-defined as the extent to which AI can work in its own interest rather than that of its owners. In other words, should economists model AI like a steam engine, a dairy cow, or an intern? Here, we define volition as the capacity for internally generated behavioral variance-distinct from randomness, adaptivity, autonomy, or intentionality. Randomness is stochastic noise; adaptivity is adjustment to stimuli; autonomy is execution without direct oversight; intentionality implies goal-directedness. Volition, as used here, refers to the subset of AI behavior that unpredictably deviates from design intent, creating managerial and economic consequences that resemble, though are not equivalent to, human agency.

title: Deep Learning-Based Consumer Preference Prediction System for Personalized Digital Campaigns
affiliations: SRM Valliammai Engineering College

detail.title: Deep Learning-Based Consumer Preference Prediction System for Personalized Digital Campaigns

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that this paper is of original research. It does not influence any other studies.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All ethical guidelines have been followed in the publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding agency is involved in publishing this paper.

detail.abstract: The current research introduces a Deep Learning-Based Consumer Preference Prediction System as a system to develop digital marketing campaigns that are more personalized by utilizing a Hybrid Multimodal Federated Graph-Attention Network (HMF-GAT) combined with Explainable AI (XAI) Layer and deployed on AWS SageMaker. The given model integrates textual, visual, behavioral, and demographic data to represent more complex consumer interactions and make predictions that are as accurate as possible. The federated learning system guarantees the privacy of the data by providing decentralized model learning through a number of client nodes, and the graph-attention system is useful to capture relational relationship between consumers and advertisements. Based on SHAP and attention visualization, the XAI layer offers clear information about the effect of features and decision rationales. Tests through experimentation show that there is a total accuracy of 95.8 percent and 15 percent increase in campaign engagement as compared to current deep learning models. The system provides an explainable, privacy-preserving, and scalable way of providing intelligent, adaptive and ethically-oriented digital marketing personalization.

title: Monitoring Technologies in Industrial Systems
affiliations: William Paterson University - Cotsakos College of Business and University of Guelph, Gordon S. Lang School of Business and Economics

detail.title: Monitoring Technologies in Industrial Systems

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval obtained from McMaster University Research Ethics Board: MREB 2014-158.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Marketing Research, volume 62, issue 2, 2025[10.1177/00222437241282308]

detail.abstract: Monitoring technologies, which are at the heart of the industrial Internet of Things (IOT) ecosystems, promise significant transactional efficiencies by making it easier to track product performance and contract compliance. These efficiencies are particularly compelling in industrial multi-vendor, multi-component systems, where complex component interdependencies often cause disputes around liability in the case of product failures. Drawing on transaction cost theory, fieldwork, and a national survey of industrial original equipment manufacturers we estimate how product performance contracts are specified in these contexts, and how these monitoring technologies can impact ex-post exchanges between OEMs and their suppliers. We find that systems architecture associated with the multi-component systems, as well as the presumed efficiencies of monitoring technologies, drive the contract designs through their potential impact on the disputes, monitoring, and contract writing costs faced by the OEM. However, we also find there are clear limits to the benefits offered by these monitoring technologies. The greater monitoring facilitated by these technologies appears to exacerbate disputes. This counterintuitive finding comports with the view that, when unforeseen interdependent failures occur, detailed data from monitoring may trigger a spate disputes over new and unexpected information, as well as over the appropriateness of existing protocols for failure metrics and remedies.

The questionnaire results were tabulated, analysed, and concluded that the attitude of locale at destination (Eco retreat) is not of very friendly environment & very distant desert places have been excluded here and pointed out for value integration.

title: Bigger Gets Bigger: The Impact of Discretionary Rating Control on Quality Improvement and Inequality
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Bigger Gets Bigger: The Impact of Discretionary Rating Control on Quality Improvement and Inequality
detail.abstract: User ratings play a central role in determining app success in digital marketplaces by influencing visibility, user adoption, and market dynamics. Apple introduced a major policy change that grants developers discretion to retain or reset their app ratings when releasing updates, replacing the prior system that automatically reset ratings with each version release. This study examines how this policy change affects developer behavior, app quality, and market outcomes. In particular, we investigate whether flexibility in rating control disproportionately benefits developers with established market positions. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that the change significantly increased update frequency and improved average ratings and market share. However, these benefits were unevenly distributed: established apps with strong reputations better used the new flexibility, amplifying their performance advantages and contributing to greater market polarization. The findings suggest that, while discretionary feedback policies promote continuous improvement and enhance overall product quality, they may simultaneously exacerbate disparities within the market. This study contributes to research on quality management and platform governance by demonstrating how feedback design shapes users' strategic behavior and the resulting market structure.

title: "The Role of CRM and e-CRM in Banking Sector: A bibliometric Review on Customer Loyalty and Performance."
affiliations: Government College for Women

detail.title: "The Role of CRM and e-CRM in Banking Sector: A bibliometric Review on Customer Loyalty and Performance."

declarations.funderStatement: No funding received

detail.abstract: This study explores evolving trends in Customer Relationship Management (CRM) research, focusing on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and electronic CRM (e-CRM) systems in the banking sector. A bibliometric analysis of 209 articles from 2002 to 2024 highlights key trends, including the shift from traditional CRM to AI-driven e-CRM systems. The findings indicate that AI-enhanced CRM systems significantly improve customer satisfaction, loyalty, and operational efficiency by enabling personalized interactions and automated decision-making. Leadership support and alignment with sustainable practices were identified as critical factors for successful CRM implementation. Geographically, research on AI-embedded CRM in banking is most concentrated in North America and Europe, with emerging contributions from India. The study also reveals a gap in research addressing rural banking contexts, suggesting the need for more inclusive studies. These trends underscore the growing importance of AI in CRM for maintaining competitive advantage and fostering long-term customer relationships in the banking industry.

title: Non-Wage Benefits and Employee Sorting
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Rotterdam School of Management (RSM), WU Vienna University of Economics and Business and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Non-Wage Benefits and Employee Sorting

declarations.funderStatement: This article is based on research funded by an IMA Research Foundation Academic Grant.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether non-wage benefits can facilitate the sorting of employees into different remuneration arrangements within firms. Using data from the largest employer review platform in Germany, we derive four main insights. First, we document that the number and types of benefits employees receive exhibit substantial within-firm variation. Second, we find that women receive more benefits compared to men and that this difference is concentrated in benefits that can be considered family-friendly. Third, analyses that exploit information on employee satisfaction and cross-sectional variation in firm characteristics suggest that the observed gender differences in received benefits are due to differential preferences. Finally, we examine whether, consistent with preference-based sorting, firms offering more variation in benefit arrangements are associated with positive employment outcomes. We find that greater within-firm variability in benefits is associated with higher employee satisfaction and retention. Taken together, our findings provide corroborating evidence for the sorting role of benefits in the design of employee remuneration packages.

title: From Man to Man with AI Navigation: An Essay on the Homo Economicus Strengthened and Weakened by AI
affiliations: Balikesir University

detail.title: From Man to Man with AI Navigation: An Essay on the Homo Economicus Strengthened and Weakened by AI
detail.abstract: Homo economicus, who is assumed always to pursue utility maximization, has been accepted as a fundamental assumption in both classical and neoclassical economic theories. However, this concept has been questioned in both theoretical and empirical studies. This article examines the approach of the rational human being on the one hand and investigates the limits of rationality on the other. In conducting this research, the article outlines the general framework of homo economicus and highlights how the approach of rationality evolves and differs within the context of real-world phenomena. Within the framework of behavioral economics, the article presents cognitive biases and deviations from rational behaviors that contradict the assumptions of utility maximization. Then, it focuses on humans and artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in the context of rational decision-making. In the last section, the potential relationship between AI and a new human species equipped with AI is discussed, suggesting that Homo economicus may evolve significantly and potentially exhibit greater rationality than before. This paper discusses the need to redefine rationality in economics as a dynamic process and conceptualize it in the new world. The paper aims to contribute to the reevaluation of the concept of decision-making in the era of AI and to enhance human ability to make more rational decisions by reevaluating the approaches of Classical and Neoclassical Economics as well as Behavioral Economics.

title: Education Choices and the Gender Gap in Labour Market Outcomes: The Role of STEM in India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore and University of Göttingen - Faculty of Economics and Business Administration

detail.title: Education Choices and the Gender Gap in Labour Market Outcomes: The Role of STEM in India
detail.abstract: This study examines how early educational choices shape gender inequality in labour-market outcomes in India. Despite rising female education, declining fertility, and sustained economic growth, female labour force participation has remained low. While existing literature links women's education to employment, it largely focuses on the level of education rather than its type. Using nationally representative data from India, we analyze how stream choice at the school level affects employment, occupation, and earnings. Household and sibling fixed effects models show that women who studied science or business are more likely to participate in the labour market, hold salaried jobs, work in male-dominated occupations, and earn higher wages. The corresponding effects for men are smaller, indicating that technical and business education benefit women disproportionately and help narrow gender gaps in these outcomes. These results are robust to alternative specifications, including inverse-probability-weighted regression adjustment. The study demonstrates that women's under-representation in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) contributes to occupational segregation and the gender wage gap in the context of an emerging economy.
