title: The Plastics Game of Thrones: What Is the Plastics Pollution Problem Represented to Be in the Plastics Treaty Negotiations?
affiliations: Stockholm University - Stockholm Resilience Center, Roskilde University - Department of Science and Environment, University of Gothenburg and Stockholm University - Stockholm Resilience Center

detail.title: The Plastics Game of Thrones: What Is the Plastics Pollution Problem Represented to Be in the Plastics Treaty Negotiations?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests. E.P., P.V.G. and B.C.A. are active members of the Scientists’ Coalition for an Effective Plastics Treaty.
declarations.funderStatement: EP acknowledges funding from Velux Foundation under the project Marine Plastic II. SEC, PVG, BCA acknowledge funding from Formas for the project The plastic pollution challenge, grant number 2020-01295. PVG and BCA thank Dr. Andreas Pedrovnik and Naturskyddsföreningen (Swedish Society for Nature Conservation) for facilitating and sponsoring our accreditation to the Plastics Treaty. EP thanks Stockholm Environmental Institute and Plastic Change for enabling her accreditation to the INC 2, 5.1 and 5.2. PVG profoundly thanks Carolina Manhusen (co-founder of Ocean Born Foundation, now One Ocean Planet) for making financially possible her participation in the Plastics Treaty to INC-1 to INC-5.1. BCA thanks the International Cooperation group at the Natural Science Faculty, University of Gothenburg for travel support

publicationDetails.detailsText: The paper is under review for consideration to be published at Environmental Science and Policy

detail.abstract:
Negotiations for an international legally binding instrument to end plastics pollution are a highly-contested arena framing “plastics pollution” as a global policy problem. High and low-ambition groupings of political actors strive to control the problem representation, a power struggle ultimately affecting everyday people worldwide and the planetary environment.

Drawing on Plastics Treaty negotiation texts from 2022 and 2024, with participant observations of Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee sessions (INC-1 to INC-5.1), we critically interrogate evolving representations of the plastics pollution problem, combining Bacchi’s “What is the Problem Represented to be” (WPR) approach with a social-ecological systems perspective. Our approach contextualizes problem representation within understanding of sustainable systems.

A minority group of countries has dominated the INC process, representing plastics pollution as a consumer waste problem, where inadequate end-of-life management of “plastic” (a single undifferentiated material) affects the marine environment. These low-ambition actors, notably petro-states, exert power over the INC process through stalling, lobbying, mis- and disinformation, political pressures and even intimidation by industry actors. Left unproblematized are human rights, just transition, effects of plastics (complex assemblages of chemicals) on human health, and transboundary responsibilities of plastics producers, including on climate and biodiversity.

These issues are red line items for petro-states, while civil society groups, Indigenous people, and sustainability-concerned scientists press for their inclusion in the Plastics Treaty. By INC-5.1, most member states supported a higher-ambition treaty, yet no treaty text was agreed. Viewing problem representations as social-ecological issues shows how a narrow waste framing is unjust, exacerbating existing impacts of plastics pollution, especially on already vulnerable communities.

title: Partisan Disbelief in Polarized Societies: Evidence from South Korea and the U.S.
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD), Hitotsubashi University - Graduate School of Economics, Sungkyunkwan University and Department of Political Science, Faculty of Law, Keio University

detail.title: Partisan Disbelief in Polarized Societies: Evidence from South Korea and the U.S.

declarations.ethicsApproval: The survey protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Keio University and Sungkyunkwan University
declarations.funderStatement: This study was financially supported by JSPS Topic-Setting Program to Advance Cutting-Edge Humanities and Social Sciences Research Grant Number JPJS00123811919

detail.abstract: This paper introduces and tests a new concept-partisan disbelief in knowledge-the tendency for partisans to believe that their in-group is more knowledgeable than the opposing party, even about basic non-partisan facts. Using large-scale surveys and experiments in South Korea and the United States, we document that partisans perceive their in-group's accuracy rate in judging non-partisan facts to exceed that of the out-group by about 15 percentage points. This partisan disblief distorts information processing: When identical information is attributed to outgroup sources, individuals are less likely to update their opinions, revealing an in-group bias that extends beyond explicitly partisan issues. Providing corrective evidence that both sides are equally knowledgeable reduces partisan disbelief and weakens this in-group bias. It also temporarily lowers affective polarization, though the effect fades over time. Together, these results show that polarization extends beyond politics to perceptions of competence, identifying a novel cognitive mechanism through which social identity undermines accurate information processing and mutual understanding in societies.

title: Need For Speed: Rapid Pricing of American Options Using Deep Learning
affiliations: and Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS)

detail.title: Need For Speed: Rapid Pricing of American Options Using Deep Learning
detail.abstract: This study proposes a deep learning based framework for pricing American options. The methodology builds upon parameterized physics-informed neural networks (PPINNs), an extension of standard PINNs in which both state variables(stock price and time to maturity) and model parameters (strike price, volatility, interest rate) are incorporated as inputs. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first application of PPINNs to option pricing. This formulation preserves the central advantages of physics-informed learning, such as being a mesh-free and unsupervised learning approach, which follows/preserves the structural properties of the Black-Scholes partial differential equation.Furthermore, the parameterized architecture allows the trained network to give near-instantaneous valuation of newly specified options without requiring retraining. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed PPINNs model achieves a high degree of pricing accuracy while providing an approximate four-fold reduction in computational time compared to exact or numerical benchmarks. Collectively, these findings establish PPINNs as a robust and computationally efficient alternative to conventional pricing routines, especially in scenarios where time is of the essence, like high-frequency trading, risk management, and market-making.

title: Heterogeneous Patience, Population Growth, and Wealth Accumulation
affiliations: Universitat de les Illes Balears and University of the Balearic Islands

detail.title: Heterogeneous Patience, Population Growth, and Wealth Accumulation

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study a neoclassical growth model with population growth and agents who are heterogeneous in their discount factors. Population growth is interpreted as the entry of new infinitely-lived agents with zero initial endowments who are not included in the economic calculus of existing agents. We prove that when capital and labor are substitutes in production and utility is isoelastic, there exists a unique stationary equilibrium in per capita terms. A stationary equilibrium can take one of two forms: a Ramsey conjecture equilibrium, in which only the most patient agents own the entire capital stock, or a non-degenerate equilibrium, in which agents other than the most patient ones also hold positive amounts of capital. We show that introducing public debt, a labor income tax or a capital subsidy shifts the economy from a Ramsey conjecture stationary equilibrium to a non-degenerate one, and analyze the resulting relationship between income and inequality.

title: Institutional Regulation of Digital Infrastructure in the SCO: Between National Sovereignty and Regional Integration
affiliations: MGIMO (Moscow State University of International Relations)

detail.title: Institutional Regulation of Digital Infrastructure in the SCO: Between National Sovereignty and Regional Integration
detail.abstract: This article examines the complex challenge the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) faces in forging a unified regional digital infrastructure. It argues that the organization is caught between its ambitious integration agenda and the potent counter-force of national digital sovereignty. The analysis posits that while the SCO has developed a sophisticated institutional framework for digital cooperation, the implementation of this framework is critically hampered by significant structural asymmetries and divergent regulatory philosophies among its member states. The article begins by outlining the strategic context of digitalization within the SCO, framing it as a geopolitical priority for reducing external dependencies and building strategic autonomy. It details the organization's evolving institutional architecture, anchored by key programmatic documents. High-level forums, such as the 2025 SCO Digital Economy Forum in Tianjin, further underscore the political commitment to this agenda, with calls to improve digital infrastructure interconnectivity and establish collaborative digital security governance. However, the article identifies several structural challenges that create a gap between strategic intention and structural reality. A primary hurdle is the profound digital asymmetry among member states, where China's technological leadership creates a distinct hierarchy, leaving others like Uzbekistan and Pakistan with relatively lower levels of digital development.

title: When Gold Meets Copper:  A Comprehensive Look at the Informative Role of the Relative Value of Gold on Global Stock Markets
affiliations: Liaoning University, Hongik University, Dongguk University and Liaoning University

detail.title: When Gold Meets Copper:  A Comprehensive Look at the Informative Role of the Relative Value of Gold on Global Stock Markets
detail.abstract: Gold has similar characteristics to other commodity assets as raw material, but at the same time has unique characteristics as a safe-haven asset in crisis periods. From this perspective, the relative value of gold may contain important information about investors’ expectations for future global financial markets. In this study, we comprehensively examine the information content of the relative value of gold. Notably, the Gold-to-Copper ratio demonstrates robust predictive power for short-term (from 3-month to 12-month) stock returns across numerous developed stock markets and global markets. We assess its performance across various economic conditions, emphasizing increased predictability during recessions, consistent with gold's safe-haven role. Furthermore, we examine the influence of copper price on overall economic growth, unveiling the Gold-Copper ratio's predictability even in times of economic expansion. Rigorous tests substantiate the consistent predictive capability of the Gold-Copper ratio across various scenarios, leading to significant economic gains.

title: Inflation Expectations and Firms' Decisions in High Inflation: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial
affiliations: Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, Sabanci University and Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey

detail.title: Inflation Expectations and Firms' Decisions in High Inflation: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We conducted a survey of Turkish firms, using randomized treatments to provide varied information about inflation in a high-inflation environment. By matching the survey data with administrative firm-level data on employment, sales, credit, and foreign exchange transactions, we explore the impact of exogenous variations in inflation expectations on firms' behavior, borrowing decisions, and expectations. Our findings are summarized in seven facts: (i) information treatments are effective at generating exogenous variation in inflation expectations, even when inflation is high; (ii) the pass-through to firms' own price, wage, and cost expectations is strong, reaching up to 60%; (iii) firms adopt a supply-side interpretation of inflation—lower inflation expectations make them more optimistic; (iv) firms with lower inflation expectations decrease credit demand by approximately 3% for a 1 percentage point decline in expected inflation, shifting from long-term to short-term loans to avoid higher perceived costs; (v) they dollarize their liabilities by increasing their share of FX-denominated debt; (vi) they de-dollarize their assets by decreasing their net foreign currency holdings; and (vii) they increase their real activity, leading to higher employment and sales, and lower inventory.

title: Short-circuiting Price-default Spirals in Housing Markets
affiliations: San Diego State University, West Virginia University and UNC Charlotte

detail.title: Short-circuiting Price-default Spirals in Housing Markets
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether liquidating distressed houses via short sales instead of real estate owned (REO) transactions can reduce the number of nearby homeowners who subsequently default, thereby curtailing price-default spirals in surrounding housing markets. Using the mortgage securitization of the liquidated house as an instrument for the liquidation channel, we find that each house liquidated via an REO instead of a short sale results in an additional 0.12 to 0.41 homeowner defaults within a 0.10-mile radius. These results suggest that policies that incentivize short sale liquidations can help mitigate price-default spirals in housing markets.

title: Why Do Supply Disruptions Lead to Inflation? Survey Evidence from the COVID Pandemic
affiliations: , , Williams College and University of Tübingen

detail.title: Why Do Supply Disruptions Lead to Inflation? Survey Evidence from the COVID Pandemic

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Firms tend to justify price increases as necessary to cover rising costs. However, standard models imply that firms not only adjust prices to cost increases, but also to changes in spending. We present a model where, instead, there is differential adjustment depending on the type of shock. The model is disciplined using a firm survey, which shows that, towards the end of the pandemic, price increases were primarily a response to higher costs. In contrast, firms report not reacting to higher demand to avoid upsetting customers. Supply shocks are responsible for most of the upward adjustment of prices.

title: The Impact of Cellphone Bans in Schools on Student Outcomes: Evidence from Florida
affiliations: University of Rochester and RAND Corporation

detail.title: The Impact of Cellphone Bans in Schools on Student Outcomes: Evidence from Florida

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Cellphone bans in schools have become a popular policy in recent years in the United States, yet very little is known about their effects on student outcomes. In this study, we try to fill this gap by examining the causal effects of bans on student test scores, suspensions, and absences using detailed student-level data from Florida. Several important findings emerge. First, we show that the enforcement of cellphone bans in schools led to a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students, but disciplinary actions began to dissipate after the first year, potentially suggesting a new steady state after an initial adjustment period. Second, we find significant improvements in student test scores in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period. Third, the findings suggest that cellphone bans in schools significantly reduce student unexcused absences, an effect that may explain a large fraction of the test score gains. The effects of cellphone bans are more pronounced in middle and high school settings where student smartphone ownership is more common.

title: The Rise of Refinery Margins: The Case of the Energy Tax Cut in Germany
affiliations: and German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), Heinrich Heine University Dusseldorf - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Rise of Refinery Margins: The Case of the Energy Tax Cut in Germany

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the temporary reduction in energy taxes implemented by the German government between June and September 2022. We use pricing and quantity data from the wholesale market for crude oil, gasoline, and diesel and find an average pass through of 80% to 85% of the tax cut, which amounts to a 3.7 cents per liter increase in wholesale prices net of tax. We do, however, document significant treatment heterogeneity over time and across regions within Germany. When weighting price effects by quantities sold, the estimated pass-through of the tax cut decreases to about 70% for gasoline and 58% for diesel, suggesting that refinery margins increased significantly during times of higher demand.

title: Which Macroeconomic News Matters for Price-Setting?
affiliations: and University of Mannheim

detail.title: Which Macroeconomic News Matters for Price-Setting?

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how macroeconomic news affects firms’ extensive-margin price-setting plans in a survey that we rolled out with randomized daily invitations. These plans predict future realized inflation. Using a high-frequency event study framework, we find that inflation and employment surprises imply significant and sizable revisions in firms' pricing plans. There is a limited role for news about the trade balance, but no significant role for other commonly studied data releases, e.g., industrial production. We also study news coverage and agents' news search behavior, finding that the intensive-margin response of media coverage and news search may partly drive our main results.

title: Household Inflation Uncertainty and Wage Growth Expectations
affiliations: University College Dublin and Bank of England

detail.title: Household Inflation Uncertainty and Wage Growth Expectations

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how subjective household inflation uncertainty around future prices shapes employed individuals’ expectations of nominal wage growth. Utilizing detailed microdata from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE), we document two key empirical findings: (i) individual-level inflation uncertainty is positively associated with wage growth expectations, and (ii) this relationship is marginally higher for low-income households. To address potential endogeneity arising from wage-price dynamics, we propose a novel instrumental variable strategy that exploits variations in forecast imprecision for highly salient consumer goods (gasoline and food). Our identification leverages the cognitive heuristic that individuals use ”round numbers to represent uncertain forecasts,” generating quasi-exogenous variation in inflation uncertainty. To interpret these empirical findings, we develop a search-and-matching model of the labor market with heterogeneous worker wealth, extending the framework of Krusell et al. (2010) to incorporate wage bargaining under uncertainty. We propose wage bargaining under uncertainty, combining the alternative offer bargaining wage bargain proposed Hall and Milgrom (2008) with the solution for bargaining under uncertainty developed in White (2008). In our model, nominal wages are negotiated before the realization of inflation. Risk-averse workers, facing uncertainty about their future real purchasing power, demand higher nominal wages as compensation for bearing inflation risk. This compensating risk premium mechanism plays a pivotal role, explaining why increased inflation uncertainty leads workers to form higher nominal wage growth expectations and negotiate higher wage increases.

title: Evaluating Search Cost Models: Estimation and Prediction
affiliations: , Frankfurt School of Finance & Management,  and University of Innsbruck

detail.title: Evaluating Search Cost Models: Estimation and Prediction

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The classic search models assume that consumers adhere to a particular method of search (sequential or non-sequential) and that they know the true price distribution. In this paper, we evaluate how well the search cost estimates from classic models predict search outcomes - the amount of search and purchase prices - when these assumptions are violated. To this end, we conduct an online experiment in which we vary searchers' information about the price distribution of a homogeneous good. For each treatment, we (i) estimate search costs, (ii) fit each model to the estimated search cost distribution to obtain in- and out-of-sample predictions about outcomes, and (iii) compare predicted and realized outcomes. We find that the prediction performance of each model is largely robust to violations of the informational assumption. Further, the prediction performance of the sequential and non-sequential search model are similar, despite the fact that the search environment strongly favors sequential search.

title: A Loan You Can’t Refuse: Credit Rationing and Organized Crime Infiltration of Distressed Firms
affiliations: University of Milan - Faculty of Law, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bocconi University and Bocconi University - BAFFI Center on International Markets, Money, and Regulation

detail.title: A Loan You Can’t Refuse: Credit Rationing and Organized Crime Infiltration of Distressed Firms

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We show that credit constraints significantly increase the risk that firms are infiltrated by organized crime, defined as the covert involvement of criminal organizations in corporate decision-making. Using confidential data on criminal investigations, credit ratings, and loan histories for the universe of Italian firms, we find that a downgrade to substandard credit status reduces credit availability by 30% over five years and increases the probability of infiltration by 5%, relative to comparable firms. A local randomization design comparing firms just above and below the downgrade threshold confirms this result. The effect is pervasive across sectors and regions, but particularly strong in real estate, where the probability of infiltration rises by 10% following a downgrade. Infiltrated firms also display higher survival rates than other downgraded firms, despite similar declines in employment and revenues. These findings suggest that organized crime can serve as a financial backstop – sustaining non-viable businesses and potentially redirecting their strategies to serve criminal interests.

title: Populist Ideology, Policy and the Real Economy: Walking the Stick
affiliations: , Quinnipiac University and Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena - Economics Department

detail.title: Populist Ideology, Policy and the Real Economy: Walking the Stick

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Populist policies are known to generate a walking stick pattern of high output growth and low inflation followed by low growth and high inflation. Traditionally, researchers viewed this as resulting primarily from populist monetary and fiscal policies that ignore intertemporal budget constraints. We show that this same walking stick pattern can also be driven by real-sector reallocative policies that are a direct manifestation of populist ideology. Using an open economy, monetary Romer (1990) endogenous growth model, we show that the real re-allocation of workers away from jobs perceived as “elite” – here modelled as researchers – to manufacturing industries generates an initial output boom but lowers productivity growth, causing a subsequent decline. In this environment even monetary policy that respects intertemporal budget constraints will generate all the classic, Dornbusch & Edwards (1990), populist patterns: a populist boom-bust output cycle, low-high inflation, and trade deficits. We use the model along with recent political economy research such as Funke et al. (2023) and recent political science contributions to organize the data as well as test its implications with a Two-Way Fixed Effects Model and a Panel Vector Autoregressions (PVAR) on a sample of populist and non-populist governments from the late 20th Century until today. Our empirical results support that the model and its real-policy implications provide useful insights for understanding populism and its macroeconomic effects.

title: Does Local Diversity Affect Charitable Giving?
affiliations: SUNY University at Albany

detail.title: Does Local Diversity Affect Charitable Giving?

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: How does diversity affect charitable giving? On the one hand, diversity can lead to increased charitable giving, as individuals may feel more connected to and invested in their community when they see the diversity of needs and perspectives within it. On the other hand, diversity can also create challenges for charitable giving, as individuals may have different priorities, beliefs, and cultural norms that affect their willingness to give to certain causes and organizations. Using data from 2010-2020 county-level income tax returns linked to the U.S. Census population estimates, I find a negative impact of local ethnic diversity on charitable giving. In particular, I document that a one percentage point increase in the local ethnic fragmentation index is associated with up to a 2.9 percent decrease in the fraction of tax returns with charitable contributions and a 2 percent decrease in charitable contributions as a fraction of adjusted gross income.

title: Unintended Consequences of Immigration Reform: Marriage Market, Intra-Household Bargaining, and Well-Being
affiliations: and Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Unintended Consequences of Immigration Reform: Marriage Market, Intra-Household Bargaining, and Well-Being

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the consequences of South Korea's 2008–10 immigration reforms on the marriage market and intra-household outcomes. The reforms unintentionally reduced foreign bride inflows. Exploiting regional variation in exposure to the reforms and using uniquely rich data—administrative records, household surveys, and registries—we find that the reforms resulted in fewer new marriages, increased women's intra-household bargaining power, shifted in women's time from housework to employment, and increased well-being for both spouses. Divorce rates fell, with a shift from general incompatibility to abuse-related grounds. These findings reveal the reforms' unintended impacts on household dynamics and broader economic implications.

title: Tariff Seeking á la Tullock
affiliations: University of Alabama - Department of Economics, Finance and Legal Studies

detail.title: Tariff Seeking á la Tullock
detail.abstract: Participants engage in strategic restraint when they moderate the policy position they advocate as a mechanism to reduce their opponent's effort in an ensuing contest that determines which policy is implemented. Epstein and Nitzan (2004) find that contest participants will indeed engage in such restraint. I develop a tariff-seeking game along the lines of Tullock (1967, 1980) and find that consumers and producers do not engage in strategic restraint. Consumers prefer the alternative to the tariff to be free trade and producers favor a prohibitive tariff. This is demonstrated for both linear supply and demand and constant elasticity supply and demand. Thus, the model is consistent with extreme policy outcomes for trade policy.

title: The Labor Market in Times of Natural Disaster: Unequal Impacts of Türkiye's 2023 Earthquakes
affiliations: Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, Sabanci University, Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey

detail.title: The Labor Market in Times of Natural Disaster: Unequal Impacts of Türkiye's 2023 Earthquakes
detail.abstract: This study examines the labor market effects of the devestating February 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes in southeastern Türkiye. Drawing on rich administrative data that link firm-level financial statements with matched employer-employee records, and enable us to track individuals for two years after the disaster, we implement a difference-indifferences strategy complemented by an event-study design to identify causal effects. The results indicate a 2.5 percentage point increase in labor market exits, a 3 percentage point rise in prolonged unemployment, a 2 percentage point increase in inter-provincial job transitions, and a 2.6 percent decline in annual wage growth. Labor market impacts vary systematically across worker, firm, and sectoral characteristics, and intensify with local earthquake severity. Losses were more pronounced among workers in smaller firms, lower-wage jobs, women, and lessexperienced individuals. In contrast, construction workers and inter-provincial movers experienced relative gains. We also document sharper employment and wage declines among workers in high-leverage firms, rural areas, and sectors more exposed to post-disaster demand contractions, highlighting key mechanisms underlying differential labor market resilience.

title: Digital Bancor: A Programmable Monetary Architecture for a Post-Dollar Global Order - From Keynes's Clearing Union to Algorithmic Institutionalism

detail.title: Digital Bancor: A Programmable Monetary Architecture for a Post-Dollar Global Order - From Keynes's Clearing Union to Algorithmic Institutionalism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships with any third parties that could have inappropriately influenced the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and computational modeling study based on publicly available macro-financial data and does not involve human subjects, patients, or ethical review processes.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant or external funding from public, commercial, or non-profit funding agencies.

detail.abstract: This paper develops the conceptual and analytical foundations of the Digital Bancor—a programmable supranational clearing currency designed to correct the asymmetries of the dollar-centered global monetary system. Building on Keynes’s proposal for an International Clearing Union, the model translates the principles of symmetric adjustment and liquidity endogeneity into an algorithmic monetary architecture. It separates issuance from clearing, embeds adjustment discipline directly into code, and formalizes monetary stability as an institutional property of rule-based coordination rather than political discretion. The architecture integrates three interdependent layers: (i) a multi-asset reserve basket optimized for systemic stability through dynamic reweighting of fiat, gold, and Bitcoin components; (ii) an algorithmic clearing mechanism enforcing reciprocal adjustment across member accounts via programmable overdraft and demurrage rules; and (iii) a polycentric governance layer that ensures time-consistent policy adaptation through recursive feedback and transparent rule updates. To preserve institutional continuity, the system anchors itself to the IMF’s SDR as a metavaluation standard and employs Bayesian updating to maintain optimal reserve calibration. Recursive governance feedback between reserve reweighting and clearing rules enhances systemic resilience by moderating volatility, concentration risk, and external imbalance. The analysis demonstrates that the Digital Bancor embodies a new paradigm of Algorithmic Institutionalism—a rule-based form of international monetary coordination in which stability, fairness, and legitimacy emerge endogenously from programmable interaction. The paper concludes by outlining an empirical simulation framework and implementation pathways for testing rule persistence, adaptive credibility, and multilateral feasibility under existing IMF–BIS institutional frameworks.

title: Socially Responsible Mutual Funds: A Review
affiliations: Complutense University of Madrid, Harvard University and Universidad Europea de Madrid

detail.title: Socially Responsible Mutual Funds: A Review
detail.abstract: The incorporation of social responsibility criteria in the selection of investment fund portfolios has gained relevance in the financial, academic, and business fields, and its potential as a driver of transformation in corporate management has begun to be appreciated. Data provided by both national and international organizations reveal the growing interest that private investors are showing in sustainable and responsible investment funds. The objective of this article is to identify some of the main advances in the field of socially responsible investment (SRI), particularly those related to the selection of investment portfolios through the application of multi-criteria decision making and fuzzy logic techniques. This paper presents a review of the literature on the characteristics of socially responsible portfolios and analyzes the motivations of socially responsible investors, seeking to understand and explain the decision-making process of this group of investors. We analyze, through a literature review, whether there are differences in profitability between conventional funds and SRI funds and investigate the relationship between profitability and cash flow, as well as the existence of the disposition effect in SRI, in order to offer managers and investors a comprehensive view for their financial decision-making.

title: Teen Unemployment: Minimum Wage and Contributing Factors
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Teen Unemployment: Minimum Wage and Contributing Factors
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of minimum wage, macroeconomic indicators, and sectoral employment shares on teen unemployment across six U.S. states from 1999 to 2019, using panel regression models with fixed and random effects and holding one state out for out-of-sample validation. The analysis isolates key drivers of youth labor outcomes while controlling for unobserved state-level heterogeneity. The Fixed Effects model demonstrates stronger explanatory power (R² = 0.660) and more consistent coefficient signs. The results show that GDP growth, rising household income, and increased employment in leisure and retail sectors significantly reduce teen unemployment. By contrast, minimum wage thresholds above $8 are associated with higher teen unemployment rates. These findings suggest that targeted wage policies, such as youth wage exemptions or specific sector training subsidies, rather than uniform mandates, can better support teen labor force participation while minimizing adverse effects.

title: The Moderating Roles of Power-Grid Quality and Natural Resources on Unemployment: Evidence from Iran
affiliations: Islamic Azad University (IAU) - Economics and Accounting College and Islamic Azad University (IAU) - Central Tehran Branch

detail.title: The Moderating Roles of Power-Grid Quality and Natural Resources on Unemployment: Evidence from Iran

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used only publicly available aggregate macroeconomic data and involved no human participants or identifiable information; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted using the author’s own/institutional resources.

detail.abstract: In resource-dependent economies, the central question is how far resource-energy channels moderate the impact of macroeconomic pressures on unemployment and how this relationship changes under sanctions. Using Iranian annual data for 1991-2024, we estimate an Autoregressive Distributed Lag-Error Correction Model (ARDL-ECM) and, via Principal Components Analysis (PCA), construct two indices: a Power-Grid Quality Index (PRQI; capacity factor, installed nameplate capacity per person, and transmissionand-distribution losses) and a Natural-Resources Index (NRI; agricultural-land share, water-stress index, and natural-resources depletion). Controls include consumer price inflation, the output gap, the real effective exchange rate (REER), and net migration; a sanctions dummy interacts with PRQI and NRI. Cointegration holds, and the errorcorrection term is negative with a magnitude of about-0.67. On average, sanctions raise unemployment by about 4.73 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from 1.07 to 8.39. Inflation lowers unemployment in the long run; the output gap reduces it in the short run; REER effects are small and partly offsetting; net migration is insignificant. Under sanctions, moderation is asymmetric: stronger PRQI acts as a shock absorber, whereas higher NRI acts as an amplifier. Scenario analysis corroborates this pattern: at high NRI the sanction effect is around 9.73 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.83 to 16.63, while at high PRQI and low NRI it is close to zero. Standard cointegration and stability diagnostics support the model's adequacy and stability. Policy should prioritize near-term grid reliability and, over the medium term, water and naturalresource governance.

title: Alt 60/40: Modern ETF Portfolio Construction Without Bonds or Derivatives
affiliations: Alpha Bet Strategies Initiative

detail.title: Alt 60/40: Modern ETF Portfolio Construction Without Bonds or Derivatives
detail.abstract: When traditional diversification breaks down, investors are often left exposed to losses from both equities and bonds. This paper introduces a simple but durable framework designed for ease of implementation by individual investors, combining directional equity exposure with "convex" downside protection strategies-without using bonds, derivatives, leverage, or illiquid instruments. This portfolio allocates 60/40 among two equity strategies and two alternative strategies: a multi-factor equity index ETF, a wide-moat quality equity ETF, a trend-following managed futures ETF, and a market-neutral long/short beta strategy ETF. Each serves a distinct role in balancing growth and defense. Rather than relying on bonds for risk reduction or options for tail protection, this framework uses liquid, rule-based components that respond differently across market regimes. The result is a portfolio that seeks to maintain upside participation in rising markets, while offering resilience during inflation shocks, rate-driven drawdowns, and equity bear markets. The strategy is fully implementable with publicly traded ETFs and requires no forecasting or discretionary adjustments. This paper connects the design to research on multi-regime investing, asymmetric risk control, and behaviorally sustainable portfolio construction.

reference: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 815
title: Public Spending and Inclusive Growth: An Empirical Analysis Across Economies
affiliations: Linkoping University - Department of Management and Engineering Division, Goethe University Frankfurt, Islamic University, Asian Development Bank and Asian Development Bank - Economic Research

detail.title: Public Spending and Inclusive Growth: An Empirical Analysis Across Economies

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 815
publicationDetails.journalName: ADB Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate the effects of different components of government spending on inclusive growth. More specifically, we consider the inclusive impact of public spending on environmental protection, health, education, housing, and social protection, all of which can conceivably promote inclusive growth. For our empirical analysis, we apply panel regressions and local projections to a comprehensive database of 191 economies between 1980 and 2023. Our evidence indicates that equity-promoting government spending reduces income inequality, as measured by the Gini index, and improves human development indicators. Moreover, our analysis reveals that poorer households benefit disproportionately, suggesting that targeted fiscal expenditures can promote equity. Notably, the inclusive effects are most pronounced in advanced economies, where robust fiscal frameworks support and amplify such effects. In contrast, emerging and developing economies experience more modest gains. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of well-designed public spending programs for equitable growth. Finally, we conduct state-dependent local projections and regional subsample analysis.

reference: Wharton Pension Research Council Working Paper No. 16
title: The Life You Save (For): Experiences Dominate Goods in Motivating Savings
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, Ohio State University (OSU), University of Pennsylvania - Marketing Department and Harvard Business School - Marketing Unit

detail.title: The Life You Save (For): Experiences Dominate Goods in Motivating Savings

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All findings, interpretations, and conclusions of this paper represent the views of the authors and does not represent official views of the above-named institutions. © 2025 Pension Research Council of the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. All rights reserved.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Wharton Pension Research Council Working Paper No. 16
publicationDetails.journalName: Wharton Pension Research Council / Boettner Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Prior research suggests that when consumers think about spending, experiences tend to take priority over goods. But does this experiential dominance extend to motivation to save, which requires long-term planning and constant motivation to achieve their goal in the future? Across two field studies and six preregistered experiments, consumers are more motivated to initiate a savings goal, save toward, and protect their progress toward experiential versus material goals. Further, analyses of real saving behavior further support experiential dominance in success rates and persistence in streaks. We suggest that this effect arises because consumers perceive experiential goals as more versatile, which can be adapted to satisfy more needs and better accommodate the uncertain preferences of their future selves. Supporting this account, we demonstrate that the effect of experiential (vs. material) goals is stronger over a longer goal period and is less subject to goal gradient effects. Further, we reveal the effect is moderated by goal specificity. Together, these findings demonstrate that goals that are either related to or framed in terms of experiences better motivate savings, making both the encouragement of experiential goals and experiential framing a useful tool for policymakers, researchers, and consumers. focusing on promoting saving and improving financial well-being.

title: Keeping the Agents in the Dark: Competing Mechanisms, Private Disclosures, and the Revelation Principle
affiliations: University of Toulouse Capitole - Toulouse School of Economics, University of Rome Tor Vergata - Dept. of Economics and Finance, Universite de Toulouse 1 Capitole and Northwestern University

detail.title: Keeping the Agents in the Dark: Competing Mechanisms, Private Disclosures, and the Revelation Principle

publicationDetails.journalName: CEIS: Centre for Economic & International Studies Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the design of market information in competing-mechanism games. We identify a new dimension, private disclosures, whereby the principals asymmetrically inform the agents of how their mechanisms operate. We show that private disclosures have two important effects. First, they can raise a principal's payoff guarantee against her competitors' threats. Second, they can support equilibrium outcomes and payoffs that cannot be supported with standard mechanisms. These results call for a novel approach to competing mechanisms, which we develop to identify a canonical game and a canonical class of equilibria, thereby establishing a new revelation principle for this class of environments.

title: A 'Scramble' for Animal Welfare Reform: Using a Multi-Species Conception of Legitimacy to Evaluate Poultry Welfare Standard-setting and Standards in Australia
affiliations: La Trobe Law School

detail.title: A 'Scramble' for Animal Welfare Reform: Using a Multi-Species Conception of Legitimacy to Evaluate Poultry Welfare Standard-setting and Standards in Australia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declare none.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research project has been approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of The University of Melbourne.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by an Australian Government Research Training Program Scholarship and the University of Melbourne’s Melbourne Research Scholarship.

contentType.other: This is the draft of an article that has been accepted for publication in the Monash University Law Review. The final version of the article is forthcoming.

detail.abstract: Farmed animal welfare standards play a critical role within the Australian animal welfare regulatory framework since they provide the legal authority on the sorts of agricultural practices and systems that are permitted under state and territory animal protection legislation. This article adopts a novel, multi-species, conception of regulatory legitimacy to evaluate poultry welfare standard-setting and standards in Australia. The focus of the empirical study is on standards relating to the confinement of egg laying hens in battery cages, a particularly contentious practice. The article evaluates the substantive legitimacy of these standards and considers how the standard-setting process affected the consideration of animal interests. The article shows how features of the standard-setting process influenced the substantive animal welfare standards. The article illustrates the susceptibility of Australian farmed animal welfare standard-setting to private interest group influence. The article illustrates how disproportionate industry influence led to a lack of genuine consideration of animal interests in the development of the draft layer hen housing standards. This article also demonstrates how changes to the standard-setting process implemented in response to strategic interventions by other stakeholders altered the way in which animal interests were being considered, resulting in a markedly different set of endorsed standards.

title: Acceptance of Medical Artificial Intelligence and the Effect of ChatGPT
affiliations: and

detail.title: Acceptance of Medical Artificial Intelligence and the Effect of ChatGPT

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: This research has been supported by the developmental funds form the Samuel Oschin Cancer Center at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center. We would like to thank the Center for Economic and Social Research (CESR) at University of Southern California for administering the Understanding America Study (UAS).

publicationDetails.journalName: USC Center for Economic & Social Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have rapidly increased public exposure to artificial intelligence (AI), raising critical questions about how such experiences influence trust and acceptance of AI applications. We analyzed nationally representative data from 10,035 U.S. adults in the Understanding America Study to understand trust and acceptance of medical AI. In the first survey, respondents indicated whether they had heard of or used LLM-based AI systems that create human-like text. Overall, 47.9% of U.S. adults had heard of such systems and 24.3% had used them. When asked about AI application in medicine, only 15.1% trusted AI to provide a health diagnosis as much as or more than a human professional or expert. Logistic regression revealed that individuals who had heard of LLMs had 74% higher odds while those who had used LLMs had 90% higher odds of trusting medical AI as much as or more than a human expert. A subsample study of 713 respondents evaluated an AI technology for cervical cancer diagnosis vignette on five acceptance dimensions, with findings indicating relatively high potential and excitement, moderate understanding and trust, and low fear. Prior exposure and use were positively associated with higher understanding, trust, potential, and excitement. The effect of personal use persisted even after controlling for demographics and general trust in medical AI. Together, the findings support the vision of human-AI collaboration to augment clinical decision making and diagnosis and emphasize the need to study the evolving sociotechnical aspects of AI technology.

title: Localised Graph Neural Networks for Aqueous Solubility Prediction: A New Paradigm in QSPR Modelling
affiliations: Imperial College London, Thalesians and

detail.title: Localised Graph Neural Networks for Aqueous Solubility Prediction: A New Paradigm in QSPR Modelling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No external influence.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No clinical studies were performed as part of this research; this research is pure bioinformatics.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was conducted as part of the first author's degree at Imperial College London.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: No clinical trials were performed as part of this research.

detail.abstract: Predicting aqueous solubility remains a key challenge in drug discovery due to its importance in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME) properties. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), have set new benchmarks in quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) modelling. Existing methods, however, focus almost exclusively on global models that attempt to generalise across large chemical spaces. In this paper, we introduce a novel paradigm: localised GNN models trained on structurally similar molecules. We demonstrate that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks on the AqSolDB dataset, achieving a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.903 compared to 1.459 for SolTranNet. We further provide the first large-scale quantitative study of the relationship between Tanimoto similarity and solubility difference, supporting the intuition that localised models can capture fine-grained structure-property dependencies relevant to iterative drug design. Our results establish localisation as a nontrivial and promising complement to global QSPR approaches.

title: Retirement Income Security in Transition: Aligning Academic Evidence, Practitioner Strategy, and Consumer Perception for Military and Federal Households

detail.abstract: The sustainability of retirement income for U.S. households has entered a period of profound uncertainty. The traditional model of retirement security—anchored by employer pensions, personal savings, and Social Security—has weakened under the pressure of demographic change, volatile markets, rising healthcare costs, and policy uncertainty. Military and federally employed households face a unique intersection of risks and opportunities. Their access to defined benefit pensions, Thrift Savings Plan (TSP) accounts, and health coverage through TRICARE or the Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) program provides structural advantages relative to private-sector peers. Yet these benefits alone do not guarantee adequacy, as longevity, inflation, and caregiving obligations extend retirement horizons. This paper synthesizes findings from academic literature, practitioner strategy, and consumer-oriented narratives to identify the primary threats to retirement income security and to evaluate protection strategies. Seven core risks emerge: (1) longevity and inflation, (2) sequence of returns and market volatility, (3) healthcare and long-term care (LTC) costs, (4) policy and tax uncertainty, (5) intergenerational support and caregiving burdens, (6) fraud and cognitive decline, and (7) housing and insurance pressures. The analysis reveals substantial overlap in risk identification across domains, yet notable divergence in framing and proposed solutions. Academia emphasizes adequacy modeling and systemic risk interactions; practitioners focus on technical solutions including dynamic withdrawal strategies and tax-efficient decumulation; consumer media emphasizes immediate emotional risks, particularly healthcare costs and Social Security solvency. Convergence on risk identification provides clarity for advisors, while divergence in solutions reflects different objectives across communities.

detail.abstract: Hedge fund investing is fundamentally about exploiting inefficiencies and anomalies especially those that go unnoticed or underpriced by traditional markets. Growing up in India, it becomes apparent how every economy, developed or emerging, has hidden pathways and informal sectors that play a far greater role than surface-level data suggests. These latent, informal, and shadow economies ignite chain reactions across sovereign credit, tax revenue, entrepreneurship, capital flows, and beyond. Building on this insight, the objective is to construct a quantitative framework that uncovers hidden asset pools and maps their systemic ripple effects specifically within the world’s two of the most prominent economies, the United States and China. By doing so, the framework enables sharper, more actionable, and fundamentally differentiated macro-level forecasts grounded in structural asymmetries between these global powerhouses."

title: Gas Flares to Green Gains: Exploring Nigeria’s Flare Commercialisation and Energy Transition Opportunities
affiliations: TIWA TALKS GREEN, TIWA TALKS GREEN and

detail.title: Gas Flares to Green Gains: Exploring Nigeria’s Flare Commercialisation and Energy Transition Opportunities
detail.abstract:
Gas Flares to Green Gains: Exploring Nigeria’s Flare Commercialisation and Energy Transition Opportunities

For decades, gas flaring has been both an economic loss and an environmental burden for Nigeria. Today, through the Petroleum Industry Act and the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission’s flare gas commercialisation framework, the country is charting a new path that turns wasted flare gas into sustainable value.

In our article, we explore the legal framework governing gas flaring and flare gas commercialisation, highlighting how regulatory measures are driving compliance, enabling investment, and unlocking opportunities for power generation, clean cooking fuels, petrochemical feedstock, and industrial use.

Flare commercialisation is more than a climate action tool ,  it is a cornerstone of Nigeria’s energy transition, converting environmental liabilities into economic assets while aligning with global decarbonisation targets.

The real question is no longer whether we can end gas flaring, but how quickly these “green gains” can be transformed into engines of inclusive growth.

title: Intimate Partner Violence in Low-and Middle-Income Countries: Insights from Economic Research
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and

detail.title: Intimate Partner Violence in Low-and Middle-Income Countries: Insights from Economic Research

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
