detail.abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a pervasive global issue, with approximately one in three women experiencing IPV over their lifetime. IPV prevalence is higher in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and costs of IPV are also considerably larger as a percentage of GDP in LMICs. We present the economic theory behind IPV and highlight some important determinants such as poverty and societal norms. We then synthesize the causal evidence on the impact of a range of policies and interventions, highlighting approaches which have been effective in reducing IPV. We identify key insights from the existing literature and outline areas where further theoretical and empirical research is needed.

title: Adaptation, Impact and Barriers to Climate-Smart Agriculture: Empirical Evidence from Arunachal Pradesh
affiliations: Institute for Social and Economic Change (ISEC), Institute for Social and Economic Change (ISEC) and World Society of Sustainable Energy Technologies

detail.title: Adaptation, Impact and Barriers to Climate-Smart Agriculture: Empirical Evidence from Arunachal Pradesh
detail.abstract: This study analyses how tribal farming communities in Arunachal Pradesh are adapting to Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA), the impact it has on their livelihoods, and the key challenges they face. The study is based on primary data collected from 250 farmers through a structured schedule. The analysis employs binary logistic regression to identify the factors that drive adaptation and applies Propensity Score Matching (PSM) to measure its outcomes. A Problem Confrontation Index (PCI) is used to rank the barriers. The results show that 43% of farmers have adopted CSA practices. Adaptation is more likely among individuals with higher education levels, access to irrigation, younger household members, and involvement in institutions such as farmers' groups. Farmers who adopted CSA reported major gains: crop yields increased by 51%, farm income increased by 58%, and food security improved by 19%. However, CSA had limited effects on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving carbon sequestration. Despite its benefits, many farmers face serious obstacles. The biggest challenges include weak agricultural extension services, low awareness about CSA, high cost and poor availability of improved seeds, and limited access to institutional credit. The study suggests training on CSA, better agricultural extension support, and inclusive financial services for better CSA adaptation. CSA has the potential to enhance productivity and resilience in tribal farming systems, and with the right support. It can play a key role in promoting sustainable agriculture in the region.

title: Labor Markets as Human Ecosystems: The Insider-Outsider Theory Reconsidered
affiliations: University of Kiel - Institute for World Economics (IfW)

detail.title: Labor Markets as Human Ecosystems: The Insider-Outsider Theory Reconsidered

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Whereas labor markets are traditionally viewed as machine-like environments – where agents, coordinated by price signals, solve constrained optimization problems or adhere to established heuristics – this paper views labor markets as human ecosystems, containing living things, namely, the human beings who participate in these markets. Living things adapt to their environment and evolve across their domains of life. Consequently, activities in labor markets cannot be understood independently of their social and political foundations. Labor markets are embedded in social, economic, political and environmental systems, and their adaptiveness to their social and natural environments. In this context, the insider-outsider theory may be generalized by reconceptualizing insiders and outsiders in terms of their relative adaptive advantages and the structural barriers to adaptation. The functions and misfunctions of adaptively embedded labor markets can be specified in terms of the adaptiveness as systems or the adaptiveness of the components of these systems. The ecosystemic approach also involves a reconceptualization of agents operating in labor markets, implying a new theories of the firm and workers

title: The Demand for Economic Narratives
affiliations: University of Leipzig, University of Kassel, ifo Munich and ifo Institute Munich

detail.title: The Demand for Economic Narratives

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Economic narratives are pervasive in the public discourse and can shape individual behavior. But so far we know very little about whether households actually demand and value narratives as information. We combine a comprehensive expert survey with a large-scale nationally representative household sample in the U.S. to examine the demand for economic narratives in a high-stakes environment of an unprecedentedly high recession probability. We document a substantial willingness to pay for economic narratives of more than 4 USD, which is higher than for numerical forecast information. The dominant motives for acquiring narratives are intrinsic, but a smaller share of participants also lists instrumental motives. Economic narratives improve respondents’ understanding of recession drivers and shape beliefs about the economy and spending, but exert only a minor impact on quantitative expectations. Our findings underscore the potential of narratives as a tool to improve economic understanding and to foster more informed decision-making.

title: Female Empowerment and Intimate Partner Violence
affiliations: University of Barcelona and City University New York (CUNY), Queens College

detail.title: Female Empowerment and Intimate Partner Violence

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The chapter reviews the economic literature on intimate partner violence (IPV), a widespread human rights violation affecting nearly one in three women globally and generating significant societal costs. It focuses on the relationship between various dimensions of female empowerment and IPV. The chapter begins by outlining key theoretical frameworks—including household bargaining, instrumental violence, male backlash, and exposure theories—as well as the main data sources used to study IPV. It then reviews empirical evidence on how factors shaping female empowerment at the individual, relationship, community, and societal levels influence IPV outcomes. Central themes include labor market dynamics, education, income shocks, family formation, legal frameworks, institutional access, and gender norms. The chapter also considers how these factors interact across levels and discusses additional drivers of IPV not directly linked to female empowerment. The goal is to provide an overview of causal evidence from the economic literature on IPV while emphasizing its complexity and the importance of a context-specific, intersectional approach to both its analysis and prevention.

title: A Change Is Gonna Come: Universality, Stability, and Shocks in Personality Traits in Rural India
affiliations: University of Bordeaux and French Institute of Pondicherry

detail.title: A Change Is Gonna Come: Universality, Stability, and Shocks in Personality Traits in Rural India

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Taking the case of rural South India, we explore the universality of the Big Five personality traits and their stability over time. We then investigate the effects of two exogenous shocks on trait stability: the demonetisation of November 2016 and the second COVID-19 lockdown. We use an original longitudinal dataset collected in 2016-2017 and 2020-2021. After correcting the data for acquiescence bias and performing factor analysis, we find that three personality traits emerge: emotional stability, plasticity, and conscientiousness. We find no evidence of temporal stability. Results from the covariate-balancing propensity score weighting model shows that the demonetisation impacts plasticity and conscientiousness, with exposed individuals scoring notably higher. The second COVID-19 lockdown exerts a negative impact on emotional stability.

title: The Labor Market in the Netherlands 2001–2024: The Long Demise of a Centralized Model
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - Amsterdam Institute for Advanced Labour Studies (AIAS) and University of Amsterdam - Faculty of Economics and Business (FEB)

detail.title: The Labor Market in the Netherlands 2001–2024: The Long Demise of a Centralized Model

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Netherlands has long been an example of a highly and centrally institutionalized labor market paying considerable attention to equity concerns. We describe how this model has been falling apart under the influence of the neoliberal ideology. Fracturing of the labor force by the rapid demise of the single-earner model and accelerating immigration, falling union density, and reductions in welfare state provisions have shrunk labor's market power centrally and decentrally. Wages lagged far behind productivity growth, job security strongly declined and wage inequality increased. This comes to the fore with a lack of offensive union power when after 2016 labor demand accelerates and the economy and employment quickly reach new heights after the pandemic crisis.

title: Immigration, Search, and Redistribution: A Conjecture
affiliations: University of Bonn and University of Warsaw

detail.title: Immigration, Search, and Redistribution: A Conjecture

keywords: sharing rule of firm-worker match surplus when wages are taxed

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: In “Immigration, search and redistribution: A quantitative assessment of native welfare,” a paper by Battisti et al. published in the August 2018 issue of the Journal of the European Economic Association, the authors inquire about how migration to 20 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development countries affects the welfare of the countries’ native workers. We raise several concerns regarding the analytical and the empirical parts of the Battisti et al.’s inquiry that bear on this effect. Calibration of a corrected model reveals that our concerns affect measurably the empirical results regarding the impacts on the welfare of native workers of skill-neutral migration and of migration by low-skill workers. A particular concern is that our calibration of a corrected model yields estimates of the tax rate on workers’ wages that are far too high to be considered feasible. We calibrate a version of the corrected model, which involves “reasonable” tax rates on wages and a budget deficit. The results yielded by this counterfactual version lend support to the results of the corrected model regarding the negative impact of skill-neutral migration and of migration by low-skill workers on the welfare of native workers.

title: Gender Identity, Norms, and Happiness
affiliations: Free University of Berlin (FUB) - School of Business & Economics, University of Maryland - Department of Economics, Free University of Berlin and National Center for Scientific Research - Department and Laboratory of Applied and Theoretical Economics (DELTA)

detail.title: Gender Identity, Norms, and Happiness

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: How do gender identity and norms relate to happiness? This paper takes advantage of the 2024 European Social Survey, which asks respondents to report their feelings of femininity and masculinity, and studies the relationships between these self-assessments, (non-)conformity to gender norms, and life satisfaction. The results show a robust asymmetry between men and women. For men, feeling more masculine, behaving in ways more typical of men, and life satisfaction are all positively cross-correlated. For women, while feeling more feminine and life satisfaction are similarly positively correlated, behaving in ways more typical of women is, in contrast, associated with lower life satisfaction. These patterns vary across European regions, potentially reflecting different histories. The results are robust to alternative measures of typical behavior of men and women and subjective well-being. The findings support theories of gender identity and reveal possible trade-offs implied by gender norms for women.

title: Firms and Ethnic Wage Differences
affiliations: Motu Economic and Public Policy Research Trust and New Zealand Productivity Commission

detail.title: Firms and Ethnic Wage Differences

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the contribution to ethnic earnings gaps of differences in the firms where different ethnic groups work. We use linked employer-employee data to estimate worker and firm pay premiums (fixed effects), adapting existing methods to deal with multiple-response ethnicities and weighting. The sorting of workers across firms contributes 10-26 percent of within-ethnicity gender gaps but affects average earnings for men or women within ethnic groups by less than 1 percent, in the face of average ethnic earnings gaps of up to 14 percent. We conclude that within-firm earnings differences are the dominant source of ethnic earnings gaps.

title: Firm Productivity and Ethnic Wages
affiliations: Motu Economic and Public Policy Research Trust and New Zealand Productivity Commission

detail.title: Firm Productivity and Ethnic Wages

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We estimate relative wage discrimination for ethnic and migrant groups in New Zealand, using linked employer-employee and firm-level productivity data, and comparing each group’s contribution to output with their share of their firm’s wage bill. We find that wage discrimination is relatively favourable for European migrants and Asian/MELAA employees, and relatively unfavourable for Māori, Pacific, and NZ-born European employees, with variation across NZ-born, recent migrants, and longer-term migrants. We present pooled and firm-fixed effects estimates of discrimination, highlighting distinct within-firm and between-firm patterns.

title: Exclusionary Government Rhetoric and Migration Intentions
affiliations: Indeed.com and Vienna University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Exclusionary Government Rhetoric and Migration Intentions

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate whether exclusionary government rhetoric targeting a minority group affects residents' migration decisions. In 2019, almost 100 local governments in Poland voted to declare their localities "free from LGBTQ ideology," providing a unique setting in which government narratives suddenly changed, but the legal situation of targeted minorities remained the same. We study the impact of these resolutions on migration intentions using novel data on domestic and international job search from a large global job site. Comparing counties with anti-LGBTQ resolutions to neighboring counties in a difference-in-differences design, we find that the resolutions increased domestic out-of-county job search by 12 percent and international job search by 15 percent. Our results are likely driven by the shock to beliefs about local social norms, as we find the largest effects in counties with relatively low prior support for far-right parties. We also present suggestive evidence that the rise in job search translated into actual migration, with the treated counties losing nearly 1 percent of their young adult population.

title: Intersecting Shocks: The Combined Labor Market Impacts of Automation and Immigration
affiliations: University of Liverpool and University of Bergen

detail.title: Intersecting Shocks: The Combined Labor Market Impacts of Automation and Immigration

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how the labor market shocks of automation and immigration interact to shape workers’ outcomes. Using matched employer–employee data from Norwegian administrative registers, we combine an immigration shock triggered by the European Union’s 2004 enlargement with an automation shock based on the adoption of industrial robots across Europe. Although these shocks largely occur in separate industries, we show that automation reduces earnings not only in manufacturing but also in construction, where tasks overlap with robot-exposed sectors. Importantly, workers jointly exposed to automation and immigration suffer earnings losses greater than those facing either shock in isolation. These losses are driven by downward occupational mobility into low-wage services and re-sorting into lower-premium firms. Even within the Norwegian welfare system, the ability of social insurance to offset these long-run earnings declines is limited. Our findings underscore the importance of analyzing labor market shocks jointly, rather than in isolation, to fully understand their distributional consequences.

title: Can We Demystify Houthi Attacks in the Red Sea?
affiliations: Department of International Relations, University of Dhaka

detail.title: Can We Demystify Houthi Attacks in the Red Sea?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research adhered all ethical approvals.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract: The crisis in the Red Sea has been unfolding since late 2023 when the Houthi rebel movement in Yemen began a relentless campaign of missile and drone attacks targeting commercial vessels transiting this vital maritime chokepoint. What started as sporadic strikes quickly escalated into a sustained barrage, endangering one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes and a key artery for global trade. However, the Houthis initially claimed their attacks were acts of solidarity with Palestinians facing Israeli bombardment in Gaza, drawing an explicit link between their actions in the Red Sea and the broader Israeli-Palestinian conflict. However, as the strikes persisted and the economic disruptions mounted, it became clear that the Houthi motivations extended beyond just expressing support for the Palestinian cause. The November 19, 2023 seizure of the Israel-affiliated Galaxy Leader cargo ship by Houthi forces marked a dramatic escalation, prompting the United States to establish a multinational maritime security coalition dubbed Operation Prosperity Guardian in mid-December. Comprising over 20 nations, the coalition aimed to deter and degrade the Houthi’s ability to conduct attacks on commercial shipping. However, the Houthi rebels remained undeterred, continuing their barrage of missile and drone strikes despite the international presence. By early 2024, major shipping firms like BP, Shell, and Trafigura had suspended transits through the Red Sea entirely due to the heightened risks and costs.

title: IDRIC Frontiers Report: Circular Economy
affiliations: University of Bath, Heriot-Watt University - Research Centre for Carbon Solutions (RCCS), Heriot-Watt University, Heriot-Watt University, Imperial College London, Imperial College London, Loughborough University, Swansea University, University of Bath, University of Lincoln (UK), affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Sheffield - Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Wales, University of South Wales, University of South Wales, University of Southampton and University of St Andrews

detail.title: IDRIC Frontiers Report: Circular Economy
detail.abstract: The circular economy offers a transformative pathway for UK industry – turning emissions and waste into financial opportunity, whilst accelerating net zero ambitions. This report synthesises IDRIC’s research on the circular economy and its critical role in accelerating industrial decarbonisation. The circular economy strategies explored in the report – focused particularly on resource efficiency, waste valorisation and carbon capture and use (CCU) – offer opportunities to reduce reliance on fossil inputs, minimise waste, and create new value chains across industries.

title: Integration of NDIR Sensing, GPS and Multi-Gyroscope Modules for Real-Time In-Vehicle Alcohol Detection and Driver Safety Enhancement
affiliations: Sharkya STEM School

detail.title: Integration of NDIR Sensing, GPS and Multi-Gyroscope Modules for Real-Time In-Vehicle Alcohol Detection and Driver Safety Enhancement
detail.abstract: Globally, alcohol-impaired driving is the leading preventable cause of road traffic fatalities, contributing to nearly 22% of such deaths. Conventional alcohol detection systems often face limitations, including high cost, slow response times, and bulky integration, which reduce their practicality in vehicles. This study presents the development of a multi-sensor embedded system that integrates a non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) sensor, a global positioning system (GPS) module, and multi-gyroscope steering wheel monitoring to enable real-time alcohol detection and driver safety enhancement. The NDIR sensor measures ethanol concentrations in exhaled breath with an accuracy above 90%, while the GPS module provides location tracking with 95% precision to facilitate rapid emergency response. The gyroscope sensors detect impaired steering patterns and erratic maneuvers with over 95% accuracy, allowing early identification of unsafe driving behavior. A microcontroller-based server collects sensor data, generates automated health and safety reports, and transmits alerts to law enforcement and family members in cases of intoxication or dangerous actions. The prototype demonstrated an average response time of three seconds, ensuring rapid intervention capability. By combining advanced sensing technologies into a compact and costeffective design, this system offers a scalable approach to reducing alcohol-related crashes and improving global road safety.

title: China-EU Trade Conflict: Implications for the Global Economy
affiliations: Department of International Relations, University of Dhaka

detail.title: China-EU Trade Conflict: Implications for the Global Economy
detail.abstract: In recent months, an escalation has been spurred by the European Commission’s decision to impose hefty tariffs of up to 35.3% on Chinese state-owned automotive giant SAIC Motor and its subsidiaries, what analysts refer to as a ‘trade war’ between two of the biggest economic powers—the EU and China. The move has been widely condemned by China, which has lodged a complaint with the World Trade Organization (WTO). This conflict, however, is not only about electric vehicles or specific trade measures but also exhibits a shift in the EU’s policy toward China, changing from what was once described as a “partner for cooperation” to an increasingly confrontational stance where China is regarded as an “economic competitor” and a “systemic rival.” This development is well-palpable in areas such as electric vehicles, green technologies, critical raw materials, industrial subsidies, etc. Since October last year, the EU has rolled out five industrial probes into Chinese state practices, investigating everything from electric vehicles to wind turbines, solar panels, and train manufacturers. The extent of the conflict has expanded even further through the latest investigation of exploring China’s public procurement of medical equipment. The response has been swift and forceful from Beijing. The EU’s actions were criticized by Beijing as ‘protectionist.’ The Chinese commerce ministry has warned that the European side’s continued escalation of trade frictions could trigger a “trade war,” placing responsibility squarely on Brussels. This tit-for-tat game is resulting in ripples across world markets and supply chains, giving rise to the shudders among the countries.

title: The Probability of Formulating the Agenda

detail.title: The Probability of Formulating the Agenda
detail.abstract: We consider a group of agents who randomly report sets of issues to form an agenda for an eventual collective choice. Under two regularity assumptions on the distribution of sets reported by each agent, we propose a stronger form of the Anonymity criterion for the set aggregation rules which is sufficient for the group to form an agenda with probability one as the group grows arbitrarily large.

title: Do Cryptocurrency Investors care about Quantum Risks?
affiliations: Institut Louis Bachelier, The University of Manchester - Alliance Manchester Business School and University of Mannheim

detail.title: Do Cryptocurrency Investors care about Quantum Risks?
detail.abstract: Although large-scale quantum computers are not yet available, their future development poses a potential threat to the cryptographic foundations of cryptocurrencies. We estimate that, by the end of 2024, approximately US$ 586 billion in the Bitcoin network alone could be potentially exposed. We then examine whether investors are aware of this risk by analyzing their response to advances in quantum computing. Conventional cryptocurrencies exhibit negative returns and higher trading volume following such news, whereas a quantum-robust cryptocurrency exhibits positive returns. Our findings suggest that some investors are aware of quantum computing risks and respond by shifting toward quantum-resistant cryptocurrencies.

title: From Teacher to Technologist: What Education Taught Me About Innovation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Teacher to Technologist: What Education Taught Me About Innovation
detail.abstract: Long before I led digital finance transformation projects or debated AI integration strategies in fintech ecosystems, I was a teacher. A real onein front of a blackboard, with lesson plans inked on paper, red pens tucked behind my ear, and chalk dust clinging to my sleeves. I wasn't thinking about APIs or blockchain. I was thinking about how to explain the solar system to a 12year-old whose shoes had holes in them and whose dreams were still forming. That classroomhumble, chaotic, and alivewas my first innovation lab.

title: Fiscal Inflation with Incomplete Information
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of Finance, College of William & Mary - Department of Economics and College of William & Mary - Department of Economics

detail.title: Fiscal Inflation with Incomplete Information
detail.abstract: We quantify fiscal inflation through the lens of incomplete information between funded and unfunded fiscal shocks. Information friction naturally breaks the Ricardian equivalence for deficits to be inflationary. We identify the unfunded shock through a pair of interconnected short-term inflation and debt targets that vary over time. Qualitatively, incomplete information alters the effects of both monetary and fiscal shocks on inflation. Quantitatively, in response to an unfunded shock, the inflation responses are approximately 40%-60% lower compared to the case of full information. Both fiscal stimulus and supply shocks contribute significantly to COVID inflation.

title: Independent Piece: National-Level Strategic Deception
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Independent Piece: National-Level Strategic Deception
detail.abstract:
National-Level Strategic Fraud: The Ultimate Counterattack of a Weak Nation

How can a weak nation pull off a meticulously orchestrated "scam" to industrialize itself—essentially getting something for nothing—without exploiting its own people?

The answer lies in weaponizing the rules of the international financial system to turn the tables and harvest the powerful industrial nations themselves.

title: WTP: Epistemic, Behavioral, and Philosophical Challenges
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: WTP: Epistemic, Behavioral, and Philosophical Challenges
detail.abstract: Both free markets and government regulators tend to use willingness to pay (WTP) to measure the value of goods. The reason for use of WTP is that it is the best and the most administrable method for (1) capturing the relevant welfare effects and (2) respecting personal autonomy. At the same time, WTP might be infected by a lack of information and by behavioral biases. There are also philosophical objections to certain uses of WTP, pointing, among other things, to the problem of adaptive preferences and to turning certain goods into commodities.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Growth Engine for Start-ups: Insights into Consumer Behaviour and Emerging Market Trends in India
affiliations: St.Mary's College, Tuticorin

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Growth Engine for Start-ups: Insights into Consumer Behaviour and Emerging Market Trends in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare no conflict of interest. The research was conducted independently, and no financial or personal relationships influenced the study’s outcomes.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article does not involve any human or animal subjects, and therefore does not require ethics approval.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a critical growth engine for start-ups in India, driving innovation, operational efficiency, and enhanced consumer engagement. This study examines the role of AI in influencing consumer behaviour and shaping emerging market trends, particularly in semi-urban and urban contexts. Using insights from secondary sources, the research highlights that AI applications, including predictive analytics, recommendation engines, and automated customer interactions, improve personalized experiences, increase consumer satisfaction, and enhance revenue growth. Start-ups leveraging AI gain competitive advantages through faster product development, optimized operations, and data-driven market strategies. Government initiatives, start-up incubators, and accelerator programs further facilitate AI adoption, promoting inclusive growth and economic development. The study concludes that strategic integration of AI enables start-ups to respond effectively to market dynamics, foster innovation, and build consumer trust, thereby acting as a catalyst for sustainable entrepreneurship in India.

title: Financial Contagion: Detecting Non-Simultaneous Breaks in DCC-GARCH Models

detail.title: Financial Contagion: Detecting Non-Simultaneous Breaks in DCC-GARCH Models
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a three-step segmentation procedure (TSSP) for detecting non-simultaneous structural breaks in return volatility and correlations within DCC-GARCH models, using the supremum Lagrange multiplier (SupLM) test to isolate multiple parameter shifts. By detecting breaks in unconditional correlations, our method identifies potential shift-contagion episodes. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the TSSP's robust performance in detecting and locating both successive and common breaks affecting different subsets of parameters. Empirical application to equity and government bond returns in advanced and emerging economies reveals volatility shifts linked to the Global Financial Crisis, and shift-contagion associated with the European Sovereign Debt Crisis, and the post-Covid-19 pandemic interest rate hikes alongside the war in Ukraine in 2022.

title: Exploring an Alternative Approach for Testing Publication Bias in the Value of Statistical Life

detail.title: Exploring an Alternative Approach for Testing Publication Bias in the Value of Statistical Life

keywords.keywords: Meta-analysisValue of Statistical LifePublication biasStandard errors Sample size

detail.abstract: Publication bias is crucial in the economic literature because it can distort the perceived strength and direction of empirical evidence, or it can lead economists to draw incorrect conclusions about policy effectiveness, theoretical validity, or causal relationships.. This paper aims to estimate publication bias in the VSL literature using a new methodology that allows for larger sample estimation. Specifically, this paper contributes to the literature of metaanalyses on the Value of Statistical Life (VSL) in two ways. First, our database has more than two thousand VSL estimates from revealed and stated preferences studies, being the most comprehensive database available. Second, we use an alternative approach to test for publication bias to avoid depending on VSL’s standard errors, which are infrequently reported in the literature, hard to estimate from the data provided in the journal articles, or require imputation approaches. Instead, we use the inverse of the square root of the sample size. We found publication bias in both stated and revealed preferences and a corrected VSL in the range of US$4 to US$12 million.

title: Landholding Size, Indebtedness, and Crop Insurance in India: A Macro-Level Quantitative Assessment
affiliations: Christ University and Institute for Social and Economic Change (ISEC)

detail.title: Landholding Size, Indebtedness, and Crop Insurance in India: A Macro-Level Quantitative Assessment

publicationDetails.detailsText: ASIAN JOURNAL OF AGRICULTURE Volume 9, Number 2, December 2025 Pages: 377-390; DOI: 10.13057/asianjagric/g090205

detail.abstract: Indian farmers continue to face structural distress driven by low income, high indebtedness, and inadequate risk protection. This study investigates the interrelationship between landholding size, agricultural credit, indebtedness, and crop insurance uptake using state-level secondary data from 2016 to 2023, drawn from Agricultural Statistics at a Glance, PMFBY/RWBCIS dashboards, and NCRB reports. Using descriptive statistics, linear regression, and paired t-tests, we identify key macro-level trends across 20 major Indian states. Results show that marginal and small farmers (less than 2 hectares) account for over 62.7% of all indebted farm households, but receive only 38.5% of total institutional agricultural credit. A bivariate regression reveals that a ₹1,000 increase in monthly farm income is associated with a reduction of 1,314 indebted households (β=-0.445, p=0.016). Despite substantial credit disbursal in high-debt states like Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, farmer debt remains elevated, underscoring that credit alone does not reduce vulnerability. Crop insurance enrollment increased after the 2020 policy shift from mandatory to optional participation among loanee farmers, yet the change was not statistically significant (p=0.099). Actuarial analysis reveals that in several states, claim settlement ratios remain below 50%, with high premiums and delayed payouts fueling distrust. The study recommends fully subsidized premiums for marginal farmers, region-specific pricing, improved claim transparency, and financial literacy integration with agricultural extension. Effective risk mitigation in agriculture must go beyond insurance and integrate income and credit reforms to ensure equitable protection for India's most vulnerable farmers.

title: Entropy-Aligned Institutional Design: An Alternative Form of Civilizational Order

detail.title: Entropy-Aligned Institutional Design: An Alternative Form of Civilizational Order

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; this work involves no human subjects or participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the model of Entropy-Aligned Institutions (EAI), which transforms the law of entropy from a metaphor into a design objective for institutional engineering. EAI specifies a minimal sufficient set of six operators-Fork, Diffusion, Rotation, Open Entry, Sortition, and Open Protocols-together with a temporary convergence valve, to ensure automatic diffusion of power while maintaining coordination. The model contributes in three ways: (1) it establishes falsifiable conditions, making the framework scientifically testable; (2) it emphasizes consistency between power entropy and information entropy, preventing "nominal decentralization but substantive oligarchy"; and (3) it validates the framework with historical cases such as the Han dynasty's enfeoffment reforms, the evolution of the English Parliament, and the U.S. federal system. EAI thus provides a cross-disciplinary master law for institutional studies and a foundation for future simulation-based and empirical testing.

title: Is The Gender Wage Gap in Professional Football a Justified Outcome of Market Forces, Or Does It Reflect Underlying Labor Market Discrimination?

detail.title: Is The Gender Wage Gap in Professional Football a Justified Outcome of Market Forces, Or Does It Reflect Underlying Labor Market Discrimination?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am a three-time national-level football player, and I play for Kemp Football Club in Bangalore, India. I was inspired to undertake this research because of the environment and conditions I have experienced myself in numerous tournaments and games. I chose upon topics which was relatable to myself and would help me make sense of the conditions in my life.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the economic roots of the gender wage gap that exists in women’s football by applying six key economic theories, including network effects, taste-based discrimination, monopsony power, and market failure. Using graphical analysis, real-world examples, and policy frameworks, the study examines how unequal visibility, unequal labour dynamics, and investment have led to inefficient allocation of resources in the women’s market. This paper focuses on the economic aspect, rather than the sociological causes of the wage gap in the sport. It concludes with policy recommendations and examples of their success in the current market.

title: Debate On the Status of the Subject of Public Administration

detail.title: Debate On the Status of the Subject of Public Administration
detail.abstract: The aim of the study is to clarify the concept of "subject of public administration" to determine its essence and content in the context of Ukrainian legislation and scientific research. The publication also aims to analyze the internal meaning of forming the democratic mechanism of public administration, which is directly related to the issues of improving public administration in Ukraine. The research methodology is based on the analysis of current legislation in Ukraine, scientific sources, and discussions regarding such concepts as "public administration," "public authority," "competence," and other relevant terms. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the systematization of various approaches to defining the "subject of public administration," including expanding its scope beyond state authorities and local self-government bodies to encompass political parties, civil organizations, business representatives, and others. The enhancement of public administration in Ukraine involves studying Western European liberal traditions of public administration, emphasizing that the primary factor of "publicness" in administration is the formed liberal civic consciousness of citizens. The conclusions of the study confirm that in democratic countries, public administration is a mechanism where the citizen is the main subject, jointly forming accountable state authorities. In non-democratic or transitional systems, state power acts as the sole subject of administration, while society lacks the ability to influence governance. Despite facing military aggression, Ukraine actively pursues democratic transformations and the formation of a modern civil society, addressing challenges in harmonizing domestic legislation with European norms.

title: Monetary Policy in a Finance Economy with Banks
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Monetary Policy in a Finance Economy with Banks
detail.abstract: I present a computable model of a Finance economy with overlapping generations and limited liquidity insurance possibilities for households. Banks provide liquidity insurance to consumers and are subjected to a borrowing constraint. A government manages the supply of liquidity performing open market operations in government securities. There are distinct shocks to the banks’ net worth, households’ endowments, plegdeable income, and a general asset-returns technology. I solve the model numerically for the dynamics of the equilibrium under two alternative monetary policy regimes: (a) an interventionist regime, in which the government fully accommodates the demand for liquidity by banks and (b) the laissez-faire regime of absence of government accommodation. With respect to consumer welfare the interventionist regime dominates the regime of non-intervention. With respect to banks’ profits, however, the preferred policy regime depends on the nature of the shock.

detail.title: Aggregate Investment, Economic Dynamics, and Predictability in the REIT Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Any errors remain the authors’ responsibility, and the usual caveats apply. The authors have no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming at Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether aggregate investment predicts future market returns in the U.S. equity REIT sector. During more than half a century from 1972 to 2023 encompassing both vintage and new REIT eras, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in aggregate investment, measured as value-weighted annual operating asset growth, signals an approximate 5.6% lower expected annual excess REIT market return. This predictability is robust to extensive controls, including valuation ratios, interest rates, other corporate policies, and investor sentiment. Further analysis supports a primary role for time-varying risk premia, showing that aggregate investment covaries negatively with economic uncertainty and predicts future economic growth dynamics in a hump-shaped pattern. While sentiment effects are present, they appear secondary, and the predictability is mainly driven by debt-financed investment. Our findings validate the investment-CAPM framework for REITs and identify aggregate investment as a robust predictor of REIT market dynamics.

detail.abstract: The empirical field study was conducted during 2021to understand the Agri-logistics and Postharvest Losses (PHLs) of crops in the Kalaburagi district of Karnataka.The findings of the study indicated that the loss due to logistics was more for the farmers compared to the field-level loss. In onion cultivation, there was only quantitative lossandno quality loss. The monetary loss of onions was around Rs.40,000 per acre-the loss of onions due to logistics to the farmer was around Rs. 34,000 per acre. After harvest, the loss wasdue to the lack of inefficient logistics compared to other factors. Post-harvest losses of agricultural produce indicatedthe inefficiency of post-harvest management. In mitigating PHLs, effective logistics services are desirable, and their sustainability is equally important.

title: Urban Work-Life Balance and Its Impact on Mental Health: Evidence from Emerging Chinese Cities

detail.title: Urban Work-Life Balance and Its Impact on Mental Health: Evidence from Emerging Chinese Cities
detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization in China has transformed work environments, leading to new challenges for maintaining work-life balance. This paper investigates how urban work-life balance impacts mental health outcomes among employees in emerging Chinese cities. Drawing on a mixed-methods approach that integrates survey data with qualitative interviews, the analysis reveals that poor work-life balance is associated with higher levels of psychological stress and decreased well-being, especially among younger workers and women. Factors such as long commuting times, high job demands, and cultural expectations around work contribute to these outcomes. This study references Zhang and Zhao (2025), who document the hidden health costs of overtime culture in China, to contextualize the broader implications of workplace norms and their influence on employee health. The findings suggest that urban policy interventions and workplace reforms are essential to promote healthier and more sustainable work environments.

title: Integrated Thinking as the Basis for Efficient Corporate Governance and Integrated Reporting Compilation

detail.title: Integrated Thinking as the Basis for Efficient Corporate Governance and Integrated Reporting Compilation
detail.abstract: Year after year, the number of organizations implementing integrated reporting into their accounting practices is increasing around the globe. This is due to the fact that in the contemporary world stakeholders demand not only financial data but also non-financial information that comprehensively characterizes the company's activities. Integrated thinking plays a crucial role in the process of preparing integrated reporting. It ensures the effective interaction of all departments of the enterprise, which ultimately contributes to enhancing corporate governance and improving the process of compiling the innovative reporting models.

title: Optimal Monetary and Fiscal Policy without Fiscal Backing
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Optimal Monetary and Fiscal Policy without Fiscal Backing
detail.abstract: This paper studies optimal monetary and fiscal policy when the Treasury is unable to provide fiscal backing to the central bank. The Treasury levies taxes and issues bonds. The central bank issues reserves for its liquidity value and pays interest expenses on reserves, but transfers from the Treasury are constrained. This lack of fiscal backing has implications for monetary and fiscal policy. On the monetary side, the central bank tolerates higher inflation in response to negative productivity shocks, because the central bank optimally chooses a lower nominal interest rate. On the fiscal side, the volatility of the distortionary tax on sales is higher over the business cycle, because the central bank retains its earnings and transfers less to the Treasury. Moreover, this difference due to the lack of fiscal backing is exacerbated by the level of reserves and the size of the shock.

title: Expected Investment Growth and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns: Evidence from REITs
affiliations: , Cardiff Business School and Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School

detail.title: Expected Investment Growth and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns: Evidence from REITs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Any errors remain the authors’ responsibility, and the usual caveats apply. The authors have no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.

detail.abstract: We test the predictions of the dynamic investment CAPM by examining the role of expected investment growth in the cross-section of U.S. equity REIT returns. Constructing a robust outof-sample forecast, we find that REITs with high expected growth earn significantly higher future returns. A long-short portfolio based on this forecast earns a significant premium of 0.51% per month in the 1998-2021 sample. We provide evidence for a novel, leverage-based economic mechanism for the premium: high-growth expectations lead to higher future financial leverage, which in turn amplifies firms' systematic cash flow risk. Formalizing these findings, we propose an augmented four-factor model that includes our new factor. This model outperforms the benchmark Fama-French six-factor model in explaining prominent REIT patterns. We finally uncover that the expected growth premium is distinct from its counterpart in common stocks, highlighting the importance of sector-specific risk factors.

title: Results and Lessons Learnt from Experimenting with Passive GPS Data in a UNESCO Global Geopark

detail.title: Results and Lessons Learnt from Experimenting with Passive GPS Data in a UNESCO Global Geopark
detail.abstract: The past decades have witnessed dramatic growth in the implementation of various tracking technologies in tourism research. Some sophisticated studies with (passive) GPS data have been conducted but have mostly been tightly spatially bound. During the multiple years of experimenting with passive GPS data in the UNESCO Global Geopark Schelde Delta, researchers have been experimenting with a total of 31 demarcated locations consisting of beaches, city centres, nature reserves, mobility hubs and other (local) tourism hotspots. In addition, students have researched the possibilities for the development of predictive models based on the GPS data. Concluding the experiments in the Schelde Delta, part of the Netherlands and Belgium, the passive GPS data used was not always entirely reliable and could be quite precarious due to the dependency on the proper demarcations of (local) tourism hotspots and required knowledge. Nevertheless, the experimenting has resulted in many valuable insights which can be beneficial for important stakeholders or researchers in countless other tourism destinations around the world wanting to or starting to use passive GPS data for similar purposes. These insights have sometimes never been available before, thus having a high value for involved stakeholders.

title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy in Professional Football: An Empirical Analysis of the Premier League

detail.title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy in Professional Football: An Empirical Analysis of the Premier League
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether the sunk cost fallacy is present in professional football, by analysing decisionmaking regarding playing time in the English Premier League from the 2009/2010 to 2023/2024 season. According to neoclassical economic theory, irreversible sunk costs should not a!ect future decisions, however previous studies in the area tell us otherwise. Hackinger (2019) addresses this phenomenon regarding the German Bundesliga and, on the contrary, does not find evidence of the sunk cost fallacy. This paper replicates and expands upon the analysis from Hackinger (2019), in the context of the Premier League. The aim is to determine whether findings of the sunk cost fallacy in previous studies can be generalized to the English Premier League, or if the null finding of Hackinger (2019) is representative for football as a sport. This paper uses an alternative performance measure, an objective data-driven rating, as opposed to the subjective rating used by Hackinger (2019). In addition, methodological improvements are introduced to address potential data-related limitations. The analysis is performed both with the modifications, as well as with the original specifications from Hackinger (2019) for comparative purposes.

title: A Tale of Two Financial Collapses
affiliations: Stanford Law School

detail.title: A Tale of Two Financial Collapses
detail.abstract: The contours of the financial collapse of Silicon Valley Bank and FTX are similar: management oversights and a failure to hedge against sudden price moves led to a typical runon-the bank phenomenon. The Bank collapse cost the FDIC $20 billion, while the FTX collapse imposed no socialized losses, with all qualified claims paid with interest from FTX assets. Despite the greater social harm, no criminal prosecution was launched against Silicon Valley Bank. Yet with unprecedented speed, the government secured a 25-year sentence on Sam Bankman-Fried, while evidence of the FTX terms of service permitting his actions was kept from the jury.

title: Scalable Statistical Learning for Economic Intelligence: Bridging AI, Machine Learning, and Big Data
affiliations: Cracow University of Economics, Nnamdi Azikiwe University and Anambra State Polytechnic, Mgbakwu

detail.title: Scalable Statistical Learning for Economic Intelligence: Bridging AI, Machine Learning, and Big Data
detail.abstract: The proliferation of massive, heterogeneous, and dynamically evolving datasets has catalyzed a paradigm shift in empirical economics-one increasingly mediated by artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). Traditional econometric frameworks, rooted in low-dimensional parametric assumptions and batch processing, struggle to maintain relevance in an era defined by high-dimensional feature spaces, streaming observations, and complex dependency structures. This article articulates a unified perspective on how modern AI/ML methodologies-grounded in statistical learning theory, optimization, and distributed systems-address the core challenges of big data in economic analysis. We critically examine scalable inference, online adaptation, causal representation learning, and privacy-aware modeling, emphasizing algorithmic innovations that preserve statistical validity while enabling real-world deployability. By synthesizing advances from deep learning, probabilistic modeling, and algorithmic fairness, we chart a path toward economic intelligence: a new class of AI systems capable of robust, interpretable, and ethically grounded decision support in policy, finance, and social science.

title: Practical Challenges in Implementing Vat on Real Estate Transactions in Nigeria
affiliations: and

detail.title: Practical Challenges in Implementing Vat on Real Estate Transactions in Nigeria
detail.abstract: The Nigerian Value Added Tax (VAT) laws have undergone numerous amendments since their inception, reflecting the dynamic nature of laws and their subject to change upon notice of inconsistencies. This article explores the contentious issue of whether VAT should be charged in the real estate industry. The conundrum stems from a confluence of factors, ranging from ambiguous statutory drafting to a lack of comprehensive review of the VAT Act's provisions during judicial determination of disputes concerning the application of the tax to real estate transactions.

title: Women's Empowerment as Gender Justice: A Case Study of NGOs in Chitral
affiliations: and Government college university lahore

detail.title: Women's Empowerment as Gender Justice: A Case Study of NGOs in Chitral
detail.abstract: Women's empowerment is increasingly recognized as a cornerstone of gender justice, yet its realization in conservative and rural contexts remains underexplored. This study investigates how non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in Chitral, Pakistan, facilitate women's empowerment through education, vocational training, and community engagement. Drawing on a qualitative case-study approach, including 18 in-depth interviews and analysis of NGO and government reports, the research examines both tangible outcomes, such as income generation and skill acquisition, and intangible outcomes, including decision-making power, social recognition, and self-confidence. Findings reveal that NGOs-particularly the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme (AKRSP), Chitral Community Development Network (CCDN), and Jafakash Aurat Project (JKA)-play a pivotal role in enhancing women's agency, fostering economic participation, and promoting community development. However, socio-cultural barriers, geographic isolation, and limited institutional support persist, constraining the sustainability of empowerment initiatives. The study underscores that gender justice in rural settings is multidimensional, requiring integrated strategies that combine culturally sensitive interventions with economic opportunities and institutional backing. By situating women's empowerment within local socio-cultural and institutional contexts, the research highlights the critical interplay between NGO initiatives, community norms, and structural factors in advancing gender justice.

title: Inflation Determinants in Kazakhstan
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Inflation Determinants in Kazakhstan

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper assesses the relative contribution of domestic and external factors to headline inflation in Kazakhstan. We confirm earlier results that inflation is primarily imported, and we provide novel details on the sources of imported inflation and its transmission channels. We find that domestic factors like fiscal policy and more recently utility tariff increases are the key determinants of domestic inflationary pressures. We provide new information on the likely determinants of inflation expectations through which domestic and external factors affect inflation. We find that monetary policy has only been partially successful at containing domestic and external pressures with insufficient liquidity sterilization, likely contributing to weakening of the interest rate transmission channel. Finally, we find that shocks are highly persistent and bringing back inflation to its target is likely to be a difficult and long process for the Central Bank.

title: Commodity-driven Macroeconomic Fluctuations
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), , , University of Queensland and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Commodity-driven Macroeconomic Fluctuations

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Commodities play a central yet often underappreciated role in shaping macroeconomic fluctuations across both advanced economies (AEs) and emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs), with the latter exhibiting greater volatility. This paper examines how the domestic interconnectedness of the commodity sector conditions the transmission of commodity price shocks. Rather than focusing only on sectoral size, we emphasize production linkages, measured by the network-adjusted value-added share (NAVAS) of the commodity sector. Using panel local projections for OECD countries, we show that greater interconnectedness amplifies the positive effects of terms-of-trade gains on consumption while mitigating the negative effects of declines. To interpret these results, we develop a small open economy model with production networks. The model highlights how commodity interconnectedness strengthens wealth channels but dampens real wage channels, shaping the overall macroeconomic response. Our findings underscore the importance of network structures in explaining commodity shock propagation and the heightened volatility observed in EMDEs.

title: Daubert Meets NEPA: Judicial Recognition and Competence for AI-Generated EIS
affiliations: Emory University School of Law

detail.title: Daubert Meets NEPA: Judicial Recognition and Competence for AI-Generated EIS
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer a distant prospect in environmental law—it is already reshaping how federal agencies prepare Environmental Impact Statements (EISs) under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). AI systems can process massive datasets and model environmental outcomes with speed and precision far beyond human capacity. Yet this very power exposes a new legal challenge: how can courts, built to review human reasoning, meaningfully evaluate the reasoning of algorithms that are dynamic, opaque, and often inaccessible?

This Article argues that the answer lies in adapting the principles of Daubert—the evidentiary standard used to assess the reliability of expert testimony—to the administrative review of AI-generated analyses. It proposes a reliability-based framework that translates Daubert’s core values of transparency, validation, and reproducibility into the NEPA context. Under this model, courts do not need to understand every line of code; rather, they must ensure that the agency has verified, documented, and justified how the algorithm reached its conclusions.

The Article makes three key contributions. First, it bridges the gap between evidentiary reliability and administrative accountability, showing that both can reinforce each other in AI-assisted decision-making. Second, it provides a practical roadmap for agencies to document and validate AI tools so that their use can withstand judicial scrutiny. Third, it reframes the role of the courts: deference to agency expertise is not automatic but earned through demonstrable reliability. By embedding Daubert’s logic of reliability into administrative law, the Article envisions an environmental governance system where innovation and accountability advance together—ensuring that technology serves the law, not the other way around.

title: Historical Anti-Fascism and Right-Wing Voting in Italy
affiliations: Monash University, The University of Melbourne, University of Melbourne and University of Bologna

detail.title: Historical Anti-Fascism and Right-Wing Voting in Italy
detail.abstract: We study how anti-fascist opposition during Mussolini's dictatorship affects postwar support for right-wing parties in Italy. We construct a measure of anti-fascism from the universe of recorded opponents, and use newly digitized historical data to resolve simultaneity between the supply of opposition and the demand for repression, leveraging the random assignment of judges to the Special Tribunal for the Defense of the State. Stronger local opposition leads to weaker support for right-wing parties decades later. Our model generates predictions about underlying mechanisms, tested using using data on collective memorialization and parental voting behavior. The main driver is social transmission of political preferences.

title: Mergers and acquisitions in family firms

detail.title: Mergers and acquisitions in family firms

declarations.funderStatement: “Family Business and Long-Term Investment” Chair at the Universite Paris Dauphine-PSL.

detail.abstract: This paper reviews the financial literature on mergers and acquisitions (M&As) involving family firms, examining how ownership and control shape acquisition behavior and outcomes. Evidence across countries shows that family firms are more selective and risk-averse acquirers, often preferring cash payments to avoid ownership dilution and preserve control. Acquirers of family-owned targets tend to pay higher premiums, reflecting control value and founder-specific human capital. When family firms engage in acquisitions, they frequently achieve superior announcement returns and long-term performance, particularly under strong family governance. Overall, the findings highlight how family ownership influences M&A strategy through a dual focus on financial value creation and the preservation of socioemotional wealth.

title: Unlocking the Investment Nexus Between Artificial Intelligence and Bitcoin: Modified Cross-Quantile Regression Insights
affiliations: Holy Spirit University of Kaslik (USEK), European University of Lefke - Department of Banking and Finance, Holy Spirit University of Kaslik (USEK) and European University of Lefke

detail.title: Unlocking the Investment Nexus Between Artificial Intelligence and Bitcoin: Modified Cross-Quantile Regression Insights
detail.abstract: In recent years, cryptocurrencies have emerged as a prime digital currency and an important asset, and the financial system is emerging as an important aspect while artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced expeditiously. Although AI and Bitcoin are among the most important topics in the world, empirical findings in this area are very limited. Thus, this study aims to explore comovement between AI and Bitcoin price using quantile-based approaches from 2012 to 2024. Remarkably, the low-to-mid quantiles of AI (0.15-0.50) and the mid-to-high quantiles of BITCOIN (0.30-0.80) show a continuously positive and substantial effect from BITCOIN on AI. When AI is in its low-to-mid quantiles (0.15-0.60), it has a large and favorable impact on BITCOIN, particularly in the mid-to-upper quantiles (0.35-0.95). The results are robust by Moment Quantile Regression and Quantile-on-Quantile KRLS methods. Based on these findings policies are suggested.

title: Following the Threads - Exploring the Discrepancy of Global Economic and Environmental Impacts of Clothing Consumption

detail.title: Following the Threads - Exploring the Discrepancy of Global Economic and Environmental Impacts of Clothing Consumption

VN/20383/2021) affiliated with the Tandem Forest Values 3 project “Towards carbon neutral construction materials: prerequisites and impacts of increasing use of wood-based materials and their circulation in the building sector (AULIUSYKE) “.

detail.abstract: Understanding the impacts of textile consumption on the environment, economy, and society is crucial for sustainable development, particularly given its global footprint and increasing demand. This study focuses on the Finnish final consumption of textiles and garments to assess their global footprint. Finland is a developed economy, which relies on imports for most of its demand of textiles and garments and thus works as a good example for the analysis of the global impact pathways. This study focuses on Finland to assess its demand-driven environmental, economic, and social effects of textile consumption using the EXIOBASE 3.8 environmentally extended multi-regional input-output (EE-MRIO) model. This methodology was applied to analyze various impacts of Finland's textile consumption, including greenhouse gas emissions (CO2eq.), land and water use, freshwater ecotoxicity, human toxicity, changes in value added, employment, and vulnerable employment. By analyzing the demand-driven effects, we can identify critical points within the supply chain and provide insights into the environmental, economic, and social implications. Our results contribute towards a more comprehensive understanding of the global footprint of the Finnish final demand for textiles and garments and offer insights into demand-driven implications not previously explored.
