This product is copyrighted by the institution that created it. The institution for this research is Washington State ESD.

detail.abstract: Unemployment Insurance (UI) take-up is relatively low in the U.S. We implement a large-scale field experiment among 50,000 likely unemployed individuals to study the causes and labor supply implications of incomplete take-up. Informational letters increased UI take-up, with effects concentrated among low-wage workers. Rejection rates among treated applicants increased, suggesting that the letters primarily reduced learning costs rather than improved eligibility beliefs. Randomized messages aimed at reducing free-rider stigma induced more applications, primarily among high-wage job seekers. Although prior work finds that more generous UI slows job finding, our take-up intervention modestly increased re-employment, as work-search requirements hastened job finding but also screened out applicants unwilling or unable to verify their search. We develop and estimate a structural job search model calibrated to the reduced form-experimental results to quantify these frictions and show that lower search-compliance costs yield the largest welfare gains for unemployed workers.

title: Multivariate Moment-Based Inference under Dependence and Jumps
affiliations: VinUniversity

detail.title: Multivariate Moment-Based Inference under Dependence and Jumps
detail.abstract: This paper develops a multivariate framework for constructing asymptotically valid confidence intervals and joint confidence regions for moment-based statistics under serial dependence and jump discontinuities. Building on existing univariate formulations, we generalise the analysis to vector-valued stochastic processes and smooth functionals of their joint raw and mixed moments. The approach unifies higher-order moment inference, long-run covariance estimation, and sample-size determination within a single Delta-method framework. By decomposing the long-run covariance matrix into continuous, jump, and cross components, we show how temporal and cross-sectional clustering of jumps inflates asymptotic variances and distorts joint confidence ellipsoids. Analytical expressions and bivariate numerical illustrations demonstrate the magnitude and structure of these effects, providing guidance for robust inference in multivariate econometric and financial applications.

title: Revisiting Information Literacy: Reflective Practices for a Post-Truth Context
affiliations: Universidad Autónoma de Ciudad Juárez and Universidad Autónoma de Ciudad Juárez

detail.title: Revisiting Information Literacy: Reflective Practices for a Post-Truth Context

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known personal or financial relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this study. The research was conducted independently and without any external influence from individuals or organizations.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study involved voluntary participation of university students and faculty members in surveys and workshops. No personal or identifiable data were collected. Participants were informed of the academic purposes of the study and consented to their anonymous inclusion. Formal ethics approval was not required under institutional regulations for this type of educational research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The project was developed with the institutional support and academic resources of the Universidad Autónoma de Ciudad Juárez.

detail.abstract: Recent conversations about post-truth have underscored the importance of examining how emotional or personal beliefs can overshadow factual information. Although many information literacy (IL) frameworks equip learners with techniques to locate, evaluate, and utilize data, they may not fully respond to the challenges arising from widespread misinformation and emotionally charged narratives. This paper introduces metaliteracy as a way to extend traditional IL, emphasizing reflective thinking, collaborative knowledgebuilding, and an ethical approach to information use. Drawing on studies that focus on post-truth phenomena (e.g., Lewandowsky, Ecker, & Cook, 2017; McIntyre, 2018) and on recent insights about metaliteracy (Mackey & Jacobson, 2019; Jacobson & Mackey, 2022), the paper suggests that more critical and self-aware methods of teaching IL can help learners develop better strategies to deal with disinformation. In particular, it explores how activities such as shared fact-checking and the thoughtful interpretation of media sources can encourage students to critically engage with a variety of perspectives. Concluding remarks highlight the need for further research on the effectiveness of metaliteracy-based programs and recommend adjustments to current IL guidelines to better address the realities of a post-truth world.

title: Coalitional Manipulability in School Choice
affiliations: University of Salamanca and University of Chile - Department of Economics

detail.title: Coalitional Manipulability in School Choice
detail.abstract: In school choice contexts, we compare stable mechanisms under a dozen measures of coalitional manipulability degree. Although no stable mechanism is group strategy-proof for all school choice contexts, we show that the student-optimal stable mechanism is the least manipulable by coalitions, whereas the school-optimal stable mechanism is the most coalitionally manipulable. These results still hold when students can only report truncated preferences, when the set of coalitions is limited, or when schools cannot be declared unacceptable as long as there are more available seats than students. In contrast, if there is a shortage of seats and students have no outside options, the school-optimal stable mechanism can be less manipulable by coalitions than the student-optimal stable mechanism. Furthermore, the presence of externalities compromise the existence of a stable mechanism that minimizes coalitional/individual manipulability, even when students are primarily concerned with their assignments.

title: Structured finance for small business loans in India: building on the microfinance securitisation experience
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and St. John's University - Peter J. Tobin College of Business

detail.title: Structured finance for small business loans in India: building on the microfinance securitisation experience
detail.abstract: Reliable access to financial services at optimum cost to households as well as enterprises is important for economic and social well-being. However, developing countries typically face large classes of financially excluded enterprises and households, owing to various reasons. Around the world microfinance institutions (MFIs) have successfully tried to bring a gamut of financial services to the door-steps of low-income households. However, small entrepreneurs and enterprises, not catered by MFIs, strive to get access to efficient capital to meet their funding requirements. There are however, financial institutions in the small business loan (SBL) segment which cater to such micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and entrepreneurs. In this chapter, we introduce the fast emerging SBL segment and discuss how the structured finance approach can be used to bridge the gap between MSMEs and capital markets through the SBL segment originators.

title: Sustainability of Tenant Farming : A Case Study of Mishing Tribe from Majuli in Assam
affiliations: Institute for Social and Economic Change (ISEC)

detail.title: Sustainability of Tenant Farming : A Case Study of Mishing Tribe from Majuli in Assam
detail.abstract: When agricultural land is unequally distributed, the land lease market can be essential in balancing factor endowments among agrarian families. Against this backdrop,the study examines the sustainability of tenant farming among the Mishing tribe in Majuli, Assam. The study traces the economic dynamics of tenant farming by comparing the cost-benefit ratios of red and winter paddy cultivation. The analysis is grounded in primary data collected from the Mishing community through structured questionnaires and observations, further supported by descriptive statistical methods. The findings reveal a stark contrast in the profitability of different crops under tenant farming conditions, highlighting the economic challenges and decisions faced by the Mishing farmers. The findings on the cost of cultivation and returns structure among owner and tenant farmers have highlighted the adjustment required in the existing leasing characteristics for optimal utilization of available resources. It suggests a critical need for policy interventions to optimize resource use and ensure equitable land distribution.

title: Peer Effects in Old-Age Employment Among Women
affiliations: Charles University in Prague - CERGE-EI, a joint workplace of Charles University and the Economics Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Peer Effects in Old-Age Employment Among Women
detail.abstract: This paper exploits a unique norm‑shifting setting—a German pension reform that equalized retirement ages across genders—to examine how old‑age employment propagates through workplace networks. The reform raised women’s earliest claiming age from 60 to 63 for cohorts born in 1952 onward. Using the universe of workgroups from social security records, I compare women whose peers were just above or below the reform cutoff. I find that women are more likely to remain employed at older ages when their peers do, with stronger effects in the regions of former West Germany, with its traditional gender norms. Gender‑neutral pension reforms thus amplify their impact through peer influence, fostering regional convergence in late‑career employment patterns.

title: Rural Innovation and Sustainable Agriculture: Insights from Innovative Practices in Nagaland State
affiliations: Institute for Social and Economic Change (ISEC)

detail.title: Rural Innovation and Sustainable Agriculture: Insights from Innovative Practices in Nagaland State
detail.abstract: Sustainable agriculture is a way to meet the needs of existing and future generations. Sustainable agricultural practices are essential to attain Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This paper explores how innovative ideas in agricultural technology help to maintain sustainable agriculture in the village of Khonoma, Nagaland (First Green Village in Asia). This is a primary study with data collected through a questionnaire and the interview method. Descriptive statistical tools are used to analyze the data. We conclude that the organic farming method and the rural innovation in agricultural technology are crucial for attaining the track of a Green village. The agriculture in the village of Khonoma can be set as an example to the world in the phase of enormous climate change and food crises.

title: Community Farming and Structural Interventions -Study from Anantapur District -Andhra Pradesh
affiliations: Institute for Social and Economic Change (ISEC)

detail.title: Community Farming and Structural Interventions -Study from Anantapur District -Andhra Pradesh
detail.abstract: A well-developed agrarian sector is essential for the overall development of the economy. The study focuses on the functional efficiency of the Foundation for Ecological Security (FES) in the district of Anantapur-Andhra Pradesh, as it produced some compelling results. The study focuses on the FES organization and its transformation of farming activities among small and marginal farmers. A survey was undertaken to collect information from 70 farmers benefiting from FES from 5 villages. The data was collected through questionnaire and interview methods regarding the education and job profiles, method of cultivation, changes brought by the FES, new methods introduced by FES in their fields, changes in farmer's life and related migration, etc. The multistage purposive sampling methods were used for collecting the data. The result shows that FES enhances the irrigation facilities, leading to the use of Borewells by most farmers, i.e., 57.1 per cent. At the same time, 28.5 per cent of farmers depend only on rain-fed. The farmers start using modern technology, i.e., 94.2 per cent of farmers. The cost of cultivation has increased, but with the subsidy from the FES, the costs are minimized, so the profitability has increased. The profits from Paddy cultivation were Rs. 5000-10000 before FES per acre, which was increased to Rs.15000-20000 per acre. FES is enhancing sustainable agriculture. The utilization of chemical fertilizer is reduced by 22.8 per cent. FES positively impacts farming and the environment through ecological restoration, proper irrigation, efficient logistics, market facilities, etc.

title: Optimal Ridge Regressions Are Singular Value Decomposition
affiliations: AbleMarkets.com

detail.title: Optimal Ridge Regressions Are Singular Value Decomposition

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Researchers often need to identify which variables matter most when analyzing data, a challenge known as feature selection. Ridge regression has been widely used to select the most important features. Meanwhile, eigenvalue-based methods have become increasingly popular for uncovering the underlying simplified structure hidden within complex datasets. This paper shows that eigenvalue methods are, in fact, optimal ridge regression models. Eigenvalue approaches offer a principled way to achieve superior penalized regression outcomes.

title: Prices and Protests: Evidence from Maize Markets Across Africa
affiliations: The University of Sydney and The University of Sydney

detail.title: Prices and Protests: Evidence from Maize Markets Across Africa

declarations.funderStatement: Australian Research Council under its Discovery Projects funding scheme (DP240101563)

detail.abstract: We provide new evidence on how changes in local maize prices affect social unrest across 87 markets in 18 African countries. Contrary to a widely held perception, we find that an increase in the price of this key commodity--which benefits producers but harms consumers--reduces social unrest. This average effect masks important heterogeneity: in areas more suitable for maize cultivation, rising prices lower the likelihood of riots, whereas they increase it in areas with greater inequality in maize production across ethnic lines. We corroborate the proposed mechanism--that the effect is driven by differential income impacts across groups--using individual-level data from Afrobarometer surveys. We show that higher maize prices improve the well-being of agricultural workers but reduce that of non-agricultural workers. Our findings highlight the importance of the distributional effects of income shocks and their implications for conflict.

title: Households in Motion: Co-location Frictions and Gender Inequality
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Households in Motion: Co-location Frictions and Gender Inequality
detail.abstract: This paper studies how co-location frictions-constraints that arise when accepting a job in another location induces job interruptions for the spouse-shape migration decisions and contribute to gender inequality in the labor market. Using data on displaced workers, I show that household migration responses are almost three times larger after a husband's job loss than after a wife's. Movers experience smaller earnings losses than stayers, but these gains accrue disproportionately to men, widening gender gaps. To quantify the effect of co-location frictions, I develop and estimate a two-location household search model that incorporates spatial search frictions, gender-specific offer distributions and arrival rates, and unequal weighting of spousal earnings. The estimates imply that co-location frictions account for roughly half of the gender employment gap and 8.6 percent of the gender wage gap for dual-earner couples. Counterfactual simulations highlight that expanding access to remote work relaxes these constraints and reduces gender gaps in both employment and wages.

title: Regularized Robust Strategic Asset Allocation under Stochastic Variance-Covariance of Asset Returns
affiliations: Shiga University and Shiga University

detail.title: Regularized Robust Strategic Asset Allocation under Stochastic Variance-Covariance of Asset Returns
detail.abstract: This study addresses a finite-time robust consumption-investment problem under a quadratic security market model with stochastic variances and covariances of asset returns. The optimal portfolio is proportional to the inverse of the stochastic variance-covariance matrix of asset returns, making it unstable when the variance-covariance matrix is near singular. We propose a regularized consumption-investment problem in which the near-singularity risk is introduced as a Tikhonov-type regularization term in the budget constraint. We demonstrate that the optimal regularized portfolio can be stable and decomposed into the product of the "standard deviation," "correlation," and "investment control" factors. Given that the optimal portfolio involves an unknown function governed by a nonlinear partial differential equation, we derive a linear approximate solution. Our numerical analysis shows that the proposed regularization method is effective even in regions of the state vector where the optimal unregularized portfolio becomes extremely unstable. Furthermore, the product decomposition of the optimal allocation to the S&P500 reveals that the nonlinear market timing effects are primarily caused by the standard deviations and correlations of asset returns.

title: History of Economic Thought: A Dialogue Format
affiliations: CUNY Baruch College

detail.title: History of Economic Thought: A Dialogue Format

keywords.keywords: History of Economic Thought JEL Classification: B1

detail.abstract: This paper essay the story of how economic and accounting ideas have developed through history, using a dialogue between Hunter and Luminarius to make the story conversational and reflective. It begins with a simple idea: both our bodies and minds depend on memory, and in the same way, all human knowledge builds on what came before. What we call a new theory is really a reorganization of old understanding. The dialogue follows how different civilizations have tried to make sense of value, trade, and justice, from the ancient Greeks and early Islamic thinkers to the Scholastics, the Spanish School of Salamanca, the Mercantilists, the Cameralists, and the thinkers of the Enlightenment and Classical economics.

title: Dialogue with AI: Analyzing the Economy as a Complex System of Economic Actions
affiliations: University of Georgia (Tbilisi)

detail.title: Dialogue with AI: Analyzing the Economy as a Complex System of Economic Actions

contentFormat.other: Author’s dialogue with AI about the book he published

detail.abstract: This publication is an edited scholarly dialogue between the author and the ChatGPT-5 (Deep Research) model, focused on the theoretical framework of the monograph Economics as a Complex System of Economic Actions. The discussion reinterprets the economy as a nonlinear network of purposeful actions rather than a set of isolated agents, with implications for value theory, equilibrium, and reproduction cycles. The dialogue functions as a tool of methodological verification: it tests the concept's internal coherence and operational closure, situates it vis-à-vis neoclassical, Keynesian, institutional, and Marxian traditions, and probes the scope and limits of the-Symmetric Model.‖ Special attention is given to interpretive difficulties arising from the use of dialectics, second-order cybernetics, synergetics, and constructivism. The outcome is a map of potential ambiguities, refined definitions, and a forward research agenda-from clarifying the micro-foundations of-economic action‖ to formalizing macro-dynamics and benchmarking against prevailing accounting practices. The publication is presented as the first installment of an open series and as a demonstration of the productivity of AI-mediated scholarly communication for accelerating theoretical inquiry.

title: Polarization for Exploration
affiliations: University of Hamburg and

detail.title: Polarization for Exploration
detail.abstract: Party polarization may yield new insights into voter preferences by directing attention to specific issues. We investigate theoretically and empirically the relationship between party polarization and party learning. In our two-period model, parties are initially uncertain about voter preferences but acquire information if they polarize. This framework reveals a novel polarizing force: parties' exploration incentives. Under certain conditions, a party polarizes only to learn the true state of public opinion, thus enabling more informed future decisions. To illustrate these mechanisms, we examine the Spanish abortion debate as a case study. Using a Regression Discontinuity Design, we identify shifts in the tone of politicians' tweets driven by rising public attention to abortion, which itself stems from prior party polarization. We further calibrate our model using Spanish survey data to assess whether polarization was driven solely by exploration incentives.

title: Climate-Related Communication of Central Banks and Bank Risk
affiliations: Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iasi and Faculty of Economics and Business Administration, Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași

detail.title: Climate-Related Communication of Central Banks and Bank Risk
detail.abstract: Our study examines the influence of green rhetoric from central banks on banking institutions. Using a sample of 437 publicly listed banks from 43 countries between 2000 and 2019, we find a positive correlation between an increased proportion of climate-related discourse in central bank speeches and a reduction in both systematic and systemic risk for banks. This may be attributed to improved transparent communication by central banks, which reduces individual and systemic risk for banks. This, in turn, supports the accountability and independence of central banks, which are negatively correlated with bank risk-taking behavior. In a similar vein, central banks that are most vocal about climate issues are also leading the way in adopting climate-related policies that facilitate the transition to net zero, which are positively associated with financial stability. The findings of this study have significant policy implications in the context of central banks' growing involvement in climate-related issues and their consequent shaping of market participants' perceptions.

title: Fast Monte-Carlo
affiliations: AbleMarkets.com

detail.title: Fast Monte-Carlo

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an eigenvalue-based small-sample approximation of the celebrated Markov Chain Monte Carlo that delivers an invariant steady-state distribution that is consistent with traditional Monte Carlo methods. The proposed eigenvalue-based methodology reduces the number of paths required for Monte Carlo from as many as 1,000,000 to as few as 10 (depending on the simulation time horizon T), and delivers comparable, distributionally robust results, as measured by the Wasserstein distance. The proposed methodology also produces a significant variance reduction in the steady-state distribution.

title: Retrofit 4.0 of Brazil CADE's Leniency Guidelines in 2025
affiliations: Universidade de Brasília (UnB)

detail.title: Retrofit 4.0 of Brazil CADE's Leniency Guidelines in 2025
detail.abstract: This article addresses the proposed changes to CADE's Leniency Agreement Guide submitted to public consultation in 2025, comprehensively analyzing the impact of these changes on the Brazilian Antitrust Leniency Program. To this end, in Part I, it presents the general aspects of the program, highlighting the expansion of the scope of unlawful acts subject to leniency, the inclusion of new legitimate subjects, such as associations and non-managing individuals, and the integration of the program with other sanctioning spheres, such as the Anti-Corruption Law and the Bidding Law. In Part II, it discusses in detail the phases and procedures for negotiating the leniency agreement, including the introduction of an optional preliminary phase, the criteria for granting a marker, the presentation of information and documents, the formalization of the agreement and the rules for the adhesion of individuals, in addition to analyzing the consequences of archiving investigations due to insufficient evidence. In Part III, it examines the practical consequences after the conclusion of the agreement, especially with regard to the confidentiality of the history of the conduct, the civil liability of the signatory and the relationship with actions for reparation of antitrust damages, in light of recent legislative changes. In Part IV, it analyzes the rules and possibilities of leniency plus, clarifying the criteria for its granting and its articulation with other collaboration instruments, such as the TCC. The main conclusions are that the proposed changes seek to strengthen the incentives for collaboration, increase legal certainty and predictability for the administrated, align the Brazilian program with the best international practices and promote greater effectiveness in the repression of anticompetitive conducts, while pointing out interpretative challenges and opportunities for normative improvement for the future of leniency in the country.

title: Tax Discrimination: Exploring the limits of ‘permissible classification’ of taxpayers in Indian jurisprudence
affiliations: Supreme Court of India

detail.title: Tax Discrimination: Exploring the limits of ‘permissible classification’ of taxpayers in Indian jurisprudence
detail.abstract: The equality doctrine under the Constitution of India applies to fiscal laws. Traditionally the judiciary, however, has permitted a larger lee-way to the Governments to evolve distinct rules classifying taxpayers. This paper examines the limits of such classification in Indian jurisprudence and the guard rails that have been evolved to ensure that equality doctrine applies even in fiscal setting.

title: Revisiting the Brazilian Merger Guidelines: A Proposal for Digital Platforms
affiliations: Insper - Institute of Education and Research, Instituto de Ensino e Pesquisa (INSPER) and Instituto de Ensino e Pesquisa (INSPER)

detail.title: Revisiting the Brazilian Merger Guidelines: A Proposal for Digital Platforms
detail.abstract: There has been a large focus on legislative changes that countries could adopt to tackle the competitive challenges posed by digital platforms. Brazil is no stranger to that, and the government has just sent to Congress the draft bill for the Digital Fair Competition Act. However, there has been no discussion about updating the Brazilian Merger Guidelines. Considering the leading role played by Brazil in competition enforcement in the Global South, we understand it is time to revise the guidelines published in 2016. In this paper, we explore how merger guidelines reflect the goals of competition as a public policy at the time they were enacted. We also show that the current Brazilian Merger Guidelines are ill-equipped to deal with mergers in digital markets. We have surveyed with professionals of competition law-attorneys, economists, and academics-to better map the most needed improvements of the Brazilian Merger Guidelines. We suggest updating the guidelines in three main aspects: market definition, market power, and the role of mavericks. As a conclusion, we propose a text to amend the guidelines in the mentioned aspects.

title: Renewable Energy Policy in Pakistan: A Triangulated Approach Using PESTLE, Hajer Framework, and MCDA
affiliations: University of Genova

detail.title: Renewable Energy Policy in Pakistan: A Triangulated Approach Using PESTLE, Hajer Framework, and MCDA

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This study used a hybrid methodology combining PESTLE analysis, Argumentative Discourse Analysis (ADA), and Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (Weighted Sum Model-WSM) to identify Pakistan's Renewable Energy (RE) opportunities and challenges, which is critical for energy-related decision-making. The PESTLE analysis was conducted to determine the thematic areas, followed by a helicopter and key informant interviews with energy experts and stakeholders utilizing the Hajer framework. The WSM analysis ranked critical factors that affect the deployment of RE. Findings reveal institutional weaknesses, policy inconsistencies, governance deficiencies, and financial constraints, which are significant impediments to the adoption of RE. s. The key challenges are the lack of administrative structures, reliance on imported fuels, and high upfront costs. The key challenges are the lack of administrative structures, reliance on imported fuels, and high upfront costs. A fragmented policy environment and a lack of coordination post-18th Amendment aggravate these issues, leading to investment inertia and a slow deployment of RE sources. To overcome these barriers, the study recommends the creation of clear policy directives, introducing financial incentives such as auctions, net metering, and feed-in tariffs, strengthening institutional frameworks, and increasing community engagement. To maintain the long-term sustainability of the RE industry, an integrated energy plan is essential to align provincial and federal strategies. The study provides a clear picture of Pakistan's RE environment and the best policy alternatives to enhance RE deployment in Pakistan.

title: Decarbonization, Public Debt, and Sovereign Credit Risk in Europe: Interaction Effects and Spillovers
affiliations: University of Bologna - Department of Economics and Prometeia

detail.title: Decarbonization, Public Debt, and Sovereign Credit Risk in Europe: Interaction Effects and Spillovers
detail.abstract: We investigate the hypothesis that a country's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions trajectory reduction and its public debt burden jointly influence its sovereign credit risk, as measured by credit default swap (CDS) spreads. Our empirical analysis focuses on 27 European countries over the period 2010-2024. We estimate a panel model that also accounts for international spillover effects operating through bilateral debt relationships. Our findings suggest that a country's progress in decarbonization, along with its level of indebtedness, plays a significant role in determining sovereign risk. Delays in the decarbonization process increase credit risk, as countries may be perceived as more exposed to transition risks. Such an effect is amplified in the presence of high public debt, which limits the fiscal space available to cope with these risks. Conversely, substantial decarbonization progress helps reduce sovereign risk. Moreover, our results indicate that these transition-related effects on sovereign CDS significantly propagate across borders through financial linkages, suggesting positive externalities of decarbonization for financial stability.

title: FOR PROFESSIONAL, INSTITUTIONAL, QUALIFED, WHOLESALE INVESTORS AND PERMITTED, PROFESSIONAL AND QUALIFIED CLIENT USE ONLY -NOT FOR PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (PLEASE READ IMPORTANT DISCLOSURES) 1
affiliations: Blackrock and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: FOR PROFESSIONAL, INSTITUTIONAL, QUALIFED, WHOLESALE INVESTORS AND PERMITTED, PROFESSIONAL AND QUALIFIED CLIENT USE ONLY -NOT FOR PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (PLEASE READ IMPORTANT DISCLOSURES) 1
detail.abstract: Despite concerns about reduced market efficiency due to social media herding and information overload, stock prices still contain substantial forward-looking insights into company fundamentals. Using data from over 3,000 U.S. equities annually between 2004 and 2024, we find that both value and momentum reliably predict future cash flows, in every cross section. While the rise of alternative data has improved the market's ability to forecast top-line metrics like revenues, margin forecasting appears to have weakened. The results reinforce the enduring informational power of market prices and suggest that cost-side modeling offers underexploited opportunities for investors.

title: SPECIALIZED COURTS AND THEIR ROLE IN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY DISPUTE RESOLUTION: A PRELIMINARY DISCUSSION IN THE WAKE OF ABOLITION OF INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY BOARD [IPAB] IN INDIA
affiliations: West Bengal National University of Juridical Sciences

detail.title: SPECIALIZED COURTS AND THEIR ROLE IN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY DISPUTE RESOLUTION: A PRELIMINARY DISCUSSION IN THE WAKE OF ABOLITION OF INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY BOARD [IPAB] IN INDIA
detail.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive exploration of the specialized intellectual property Intellectual Property (IP) Courts in India, particularly focusing on the change in the IP regime post the abolition of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB), and the Intellectual Property Divisions created in its aftermath. The Paper tries to study the development of the new IPDs in India, dedicated to resolving IP disputes against the backdrop of the abolition of IPAB. Delving into the intricacies surrounding specialized courts, it also analyzes the evolution, functioning, and eventual demise of the IPAB, while questioning the absence of a TRIPS agreement mandate for such specialist courts. Through a critical and doctrinal discourse, this paper evaluates the contribution of specialized courts to IP dispute resolution in other jurisdictions and debates whether the abolition of the IPAB aligns with the trajectory of IP litigation courts in India. This scholarly examination aims to provide a holistic understanding of the role and significance of specialized courts in shaping the future of IP dispute resolution keeping in consideration, the contemporary and dynamic developments.

title: Factors That Influence Perceptions of Research Quality in Economics
affiliations: University of Wyoming and University of Wyoming - College of Business - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Factors That Influence Perceptions of Research Quality in Economics
detail.abstract: We designed an online survey experiment to examine how academic economists assess research quality. Participants were randomly assigned to view one of six economics manuscripts cover pages that varied by document editor (Microsoft Word vs. LaTeX) and the inclusion of a spelling or grammar error. Several insights emerge. Although many participants believe that papers written in LaTeX are viewed more favorably than those written in Word, there is little evidence of this. In contrast, the presence of a single spelling or grammar error reduces perceptions of research impact, competence, and even the quality and importance of the underlying research question itself.

title: Inefficiencies in the Securities Lending Market
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, University of Kiel - Institute for Quantitative Business and Economics Research (QBER) and

detail.title: Inefficiencies in the Securities Lending Market
detail.abstract: In contrast with a general trend of declining trading frictions, over the last several decades the cost of borrowing securities for short-selling has increased dramatically. Using a portfolio approach, we show that as the borrow costs have increased so has the mispricing associated with portfolios of high-borrow-cost names. This decline in market efficiency has resulted from a lack of competition in the intermediation chain that links share lenders with borrowers, and a growing and rational unwillingness among institutional investors to hold and lend high-borrow-cost names. Since 2020, we estimate that the inefficiencies associated with these frictions have exceeded $300 Million/day.

title: Energy market volatility during US-China tariff escalation: Evidence from event study
affiliations: Bangladesh Bank

detail.title: Energy market volatility during US-China tariff escalation: Evidence from event study
detail.abstract: This study examines how reciprocal tariff escalations between the US and China affect their energy market volatility. The results show that tariff announcements significantly increased volatility in both markets, with the Chinese energy markets exhibiting stronger pre-event reactions and larger overall shocks. This research contributes to the understanding of asymmetric pre-event reactions in energy markets to tariff announcements, specifically showing that Chinese energy markets exhibit stronger anticipatory responses compared to the US market.

title: Exploring Generative AI in Accounting: Information Production and Consumption
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business, HKUST Business School, Rutgers Business School at Newark and New Brunswick and Harvard Business School

detail.title: Exploring Generative AI in Accounting: Information Production and Consumption
detail.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) are changing how various participants in capital markets produce, disseminate, and consume information. This paper synthesizes key themes in the emerging accounting literature on artificial intelligence (AI) and uses them to discuss six studies presented at the 2025 Journal of Accounting Research (JAR) Conference. These studies provide early evidence on GenAI’s impact across the lifecycle of information production and consumption: (1) its role in producing information, such as preparing regulatory filings, recording accounting transactions, and generating reports for capital market intermediaries, (2) its use by investors in consuming information and the resulting market consequences, as well as (3) the limitations and biases of GenAI models, and potential solutions. To organize these insights, we situate these papers in a two-part taxonomy of AI in accounting research – AI as a tool and AI as a subject of inquiry – and propose an agenda for future research.

title: Too Much of a Good Thing? Endogenous Human Capital and Nonlinear Growth Beyond the Middle-Income Trap

detail.title: Too Much of a Good Thing? Endogenous Human Capital and Nonlinear Growth Beyond the Middle-Income Trap
detail.abstract: This paper develops a nonlinear growth model to examine how human capital shapes long-run growth and convergence, with particular attention to the dynamics of the middle-income trap. Human capital is modelled as a determinant of absorptive capacity, enhancing economies' ability to adopt and utilize advanced technologies. While retaining the core logic of the neoclassical framework, the model relaxes the constant-elasticity assumption, allowing the productivity effect of education to vary endogenously with its level. This captures both saturation and composition effects that shape convergence trajectories and govern the transition from imitation to innovation. Empirically, the analysis combines a production-function and a macro-Mincerian specification and employs a rolling-threshold estimation strategy that mitigates endogeneity in both covariates and threshold variables. The results show that human capital promotes growth at low levels, consistent with technology-driven catch-up, but its marginal effect declines and may even turn negative beyond a critical schooling threshold. Higher initial education also amplifies the responsiveness of growth to initial income, implying that convergence may slow or even reverse at middle-income stages. This reconciles conflicting evidence in the growth literature and suggests that the middle-income trap arises when educational expansion is not accompanied by improvements in technological adaptability and institutional capacity.

title: A Variational Approach to Portfolio Choice
affiliations: Dublin City University - School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Michigan at Ann Arbor and Dublin City University

detail.title: A Variational Approach to Portfolio Choice

declarations.funderStatement: Partially supported by SFI (16/IA/4443).

detail.abstract: We develop a variational approach to solve infinite-horizon consumption-investment problems for isoelastic investors in complete markets with any number of assets and stochastic investment opportunities driven by a scalar diffusion. We identify a strictly convex functional whose unique minimizer coincides with the optimal wealth-consumption ratio and yields the optimal portfolio explicitly. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by computing optimal consumption-investment policies through gradient-descent in models featuring nonlinear predictability, stochastic volatility, and interest-rate risk. The method combines verification with numerical tractability and yields accurate solutions in analytically intractable models.

title: EPU diversity, corporate investments, and corporate governance
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, NTNU Business School and Pennsylvania State University - School of Graduate Professional Studies (SGPS)

detail.title: EPU diversity, corporate investments, and corporate governance
detail.abstract: We examine a critical aspect of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) that has been largely overlooked-the diversity of uncertainty (or EPU diversity). Firms encounter higher EPU diversity when uncertainty arises from many different areas at once, while uncertainty concentrated in just a few areas leads to lower EPU diversity. Dealing with multiple distinct areas of uncertainty is inherently more complex and riskier. Supporting this notion, our extensive analysis based on nearly 300,000 observations reveals that firms exercise greater caution and significantly reduce corporate investments and R&D intensity when confronting multiple sources of EPU. Notably, the impact of EPU diversity on corporate investments persists even after accounting for the overall level of EPU, indicating its separate and distinct significance. Importantly, we find that the negative effect of EPU diversity on corporate investments is significantly alleviated in firms with a greater presence of independent and female directors, implying that the reduction in investments that can be attributed to EPU diversity is at least partially motivated by agency conflicts.

title: Internal Assurance as a Mechanism Contributing to the Compilation of High-Quality Non-Financial Reporting

detail.title: Internal Assurance as a Mechanism Contributing to the Compilation of High-Quality Non-Financial Reporting
detail.abstract: Currently, enterprises operating in various sectors of the economy have efficiently functioning departments that are engaged in the internal assurance of non-financial and integrated reporting which is becoming increasingly popular. Their activities could significantly contribute to implementing and developing such reporting within the organization as well as to ensuring the high quality of corporate reporting containing non-financial information. The effective operation of this department allows external auditors to benefit from its work, which optimizes the process of the external assurance of non-financial reporting.

title: Biodiversity Co-Benefits in Carbon Markets? Evidence from Voluntary Offset Projects
affiliations: and Columbia University

detail.title: Biodiversity Co-Benefits in Carbon Markets? Evidence from Voluntary Offset Projects
detail.abstract: The ongoing Holocene Extinction marks the fastest rate of species loss in human history. In the absence of effective public policies, nature-based solutions implemented through market mechanisms-most notably carbon offsets-have emerged as a rapidly growing asset class that often promote biodiversity co-benefits for investors. This study provides the first systematic evidence on how voluntary carbon offsets impact habitat quality. We compile the largest extant dataset of voluntary carbon offset projects and link them to high-resolution satellite-derived measures of habitat integrity in local ecosystems. Contrary to asserted co-benefits, we find carbon offset projects are associated with a 3.7% increase in habitat disturbance, as measured by the Human Influence Index (HII). Land-use analyses show that these projects tend to accelerate the conversion of biodiverse shrublands and less-dense forests into pastures and simplified landscapes, implying reduced habitat integrity and ecological trade-offs. We examine impact heterogeneity by ecosystem condition, certifications, stated co-benefits, protected area overlap, registry, and rating coverage, but still find no evidence of improved habitats. Nor do alternative habitat measures, the Bioclimate Ecosystem Resilience Index and the Biodiversity Habitat Index, show measurable improvement following offset projects. We conclude that voluntary carbon markets have ecological performance gaps and information frictions relevant to both investors and offset market governance.

title: Multi-level Matching Markets
affiliations: and University of Chile - Department of Economics

detail.title: Multi-level Matching Markets
detail.abstract: In a multi-level matching market, agents participate in two centralized assignment process over time in order to obtain placements at institutions that they consider complementary. In this context, we aim to understand how the interrelationship between the underlying clearinghouses influences agents' behavior. By identifying agents with students, and institutions with high schools or colleges, we analyze the compatibility between strategy-proofness, stability, and efficiency when colleges may prioritize students considering their secondary education and students' preferences for colleges may depend on their high school placement. We show that many multi-level matching markets have no stable mechanism less manipulable than another. Moreover, the stable mechanism that implements the student-optimal deferred acceptance algorithm in each clearinghouse---denoted by DA*---is the only one that can be strategy-proof, but strong assumptions on school priorities are required to ensure this property. However, a student can stop manipulating DA* when a limit is imposed on the number of reporting schools. Although DA* cannot be Pareto dominated by another stable mechanism, its inefficiency might not be mitigated without harming some students.

title: The Effect of Private vs Shared Rooms on Nursing Home Resident Health Outcomes

detail.title: The Effect of Private vs Shared Rooms on Nursing Home Resident Health Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received funding support from a University of Michigan Rackham Graduate Student Research Grant and Department of Economics Graduate Research Award.

detail.abstract: Nursing home care presents a significant fiscal challenge in the U.S., with an aging population increasing demand and an industry plagued by decades of poor quality of care. With the need for systemic change spotlighted by the Covid-19 pandemic, one proposed solution is more private rooms. Despite growing interest, policymakers lack critical evidence required to determine whether policy should incentivize nursing homes to provide more private rooms: do private rooms actually improve residents' health? This study provides the first causal estimates of the effect of receiving a private room on post-acute nursing home residents' health outcomes. First, using standardized clinical assessments that list residents' room number, I implement a novel method to determine whether residents' rooms are private or shared - data that is otherwise unavailable. Second, to address concerns of selection into room types within nursing homes, I use a new instrumental variable for the room type residents receive: the availability of private rooms in the nursing home on the day before the resident enters. Among ∼380,000 post-acute care residents across the U.S. in 2017-2019, I do not find evidence that receiving a private room improves health outcomes, including mortality, hospital readmission, discharge to home, length of stay, and resident mood. If anything, estimates are suggestive of private rooms potentially being worse for post-acute resident health, with private room receipt leading to lower probability of discharge directly to home, within 30, 60, and 90 days after nursing home entry. These results imply that policymakers seeking to improve post-acute resident health should consider prioritizing other proven nursing home quality improvement interventions.
